arXiv:0804.3876v1 [quant-ph] 24 Apr 2008

Local asymptotic normality for finite dimensional quantum systems

Jonas Kahn Affiliation:  Université Paris-Sud 11, Département de MathématiquesBât 425, 91405 Orsay Cedex, France    Mădălin Guţă Affiliation:  University of Nottingham, School of Mathematical SciencesUniversity Park, NG7 2RD, Nottingham, U.K.
Abstract

We extend our previous results on local asymptotic normality (LAN) for qubits [18, 15] to quantum systems of arbitrary finite dimension dd. LAN means that the quantum statistical model consisting of nn identically prepared dd-dimensional systems with joint state ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n} converges as n→∞n\to\infty to a statistical model consisting of classical and quantum Gaussian variables with fixed and known covariance matrix, and unknown means related to the parameters of the density matrix ρ\rho. Remarkably, the limit model splits into a product of a classical Gaussian with mean equal to the diagonal parameters, and independent harmonic oscillators prepared in thermal equilibrium states displaced by an amount proportional to the off-diagonal elements.

As in the qubits case [15], LAN is the main ingredient in devising a general two step adaptive procedure for the optimal estimation of completely unknown dd-dimensional quantum states. This measurement strategy shall be described in a forthcoming paper [17].

1 Introduction

Quantum statistics deals with problems of statistical inference arising in quantum mechanics. The first significant results in this area appeared in the seventies and tackled issues such as quantum Cramér-Rao bounds for unbiased estimators, optimal estimation for families of states possessing a group symmetry, estimation of Gaussian states, optimal discrimination between non-commuting states. It is impossible to list all contributions but the following references may give the flavour of these developments [26, 48, 47, 7, 8, 28]. The more recent theoretical advances [22, 23, 35, 6, 2, 3] are closely related to the rapid development of quantum information and quantum engineering, and are often accompanied by practical implementations [1, 19, 40, 39].

An important topic in quantum statistics is that of optimal estimation of an unknown state using the results of measurements performed on nn identically prepared quantum systems [32, 9, 45, 13, 30, 4, 25, 24, 5, 12]. In the case of two dimensional systems, or qubits, the problem has been solved explicitly in the Bayesian set-up, in the particular case of an invariant prior and figure of merit based on the fidelity distance between states [5]. However the method used there does not work for more general priors, loss functions, or higher dimensions. In the pointwise approach, Hayashi and Matsumoto [25] showed that the Holevo bound [28] for the variance of locally unbiased estimators can be achieved asymptotically, and provided a sequence of measurements with this property. Their results, building on earlier work [21, 20], indicate for the first time the emergence of a Gaussian limit in the problem of optimal state estimation for qubits. The extension to dd-dimensional case is analysed by Matsumoto in [33].

In [18, 15] we performed a detailed analysis of this phenomenon (again for qubits), and showed that we deal with the quantum generalization of an important concept in mathematical statistics called local asymptotic normality. As a corollary, we devised a two steps adaptive measurement strategy for state estimation which is asymptotically optimal for a large class of loss functions and priors, and could be practically implemented using continuous-time measurements. In ‘classical statistics’, the idea of approximating a sequence of statistical models by a family of Gaussian distributions appeared in [46], and was fully developed by Le Cam [31] who coined the term “local asymptotic normality”. Among the many applications we mention its role in asymptotic optimality theory and in proving the asymptotic normality of certain estimators such as the maximum likelihood estimator. The aim of this paper is to extend the results of [18, 15] to systems of arbitrary dimension d<∞d<\infty, and thus provide the main tool for solving the open problem of optimal state estimation for dd-dimensional quantum systems [17].

Before stating the main result of the paper we will explain briefly the meaning of local asymptotic normality for two dimensional systems [18, 15]. We are given nn qubits identically prepared in an unknown state ρ\rho. Asymptotic normality means that for large nn we can encode the statistical information contained in the state ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n} into a Gaussian model consisting of a classical random variable with distribution N⁡(u,I−1)N(u,I^{-1}), and a quantum harmonic oscillator prepared in a (Gaussian) displaced thermal state Φζ\Phi_{\zeta}. The term local refers to how ρ\rho is related to the parameters θ=(u,ζ)\theta=(u,\zeta), as explained below.

For a more precise formulation let us parametrise the qubit states by their Bloch vectors ρ​(r→)=12​(𝟏+r→​σ→)\rho(\overrightarrow{r})=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{1}+\overrightarrow{r}\overrightarrow{\sigma}) where σ→=(σx,σy,σz)\overrightarrow{\sigma}=(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z}) are the Pauli matrices. The neighborhood of the state ρ0\rho_{0} with r0→=(0,0,2​μ−1)\overrightarrow{r_{0}}=(0,0,2\mu-1) and 1/2<μ<11/2<\mu<1, is a three-dimensional ball parametrised by the deviation u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} of diagonal elements and ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C} of the off-diagonal ones

ρθ=(μ+uζ∗ζ1−μ−u),θ=(u,ζ)∈ℝ×ℂ.\rho_{\theta}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mu+u&\zeta^{*}\\ \zeta&1-\mu-u\end{array}\right),\qquad\theta=(u,\zeta)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{C}. (1.1)

Note that ρ0\rho_{0} is to be considered fixed and known but otherwise arbitrary, and can be taken to be diagonal without any loss of generality. Consider now nn identically prepared qubits whose individual states are in a neighborhood of ρ0\rho_{0} of size 1/n1/\sqrt{n}, so that their joint state is ρθn:=[ρθ/n]⊗n\rho^{n}_{\theta}:=\left[\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}\right]^{\otimes n} for some unknown θ\theta. We would like to understand the structure of the family (statistical experiment)

𝒬n:={ρθn:‖θ‖≤C},\mathcal{Q}_{n}:=\{\rho^{n}_{\theta}:\|\theta\|\leq C\}, (1.2)

as a whole, more precisely what is its asymptotic behavior as n→∞n\to\infty ?

For this we consider a quantum harmonic oscillator with position and momentum operators satisfying the commutation relations [𝐐,𝐏]=i​𝟏[{\bf Q},{\bf P}]=i\mathbf{1}. We denote by {|n⟩,n≥0}\{|n\rangle,n\geq 0\} the eigenbasis of the number operator and define the thermal equilibrium state

Φ=(1−e−β)​∑k=0∞e−k​β​|k⟩​⟨k|,e−β=1−μμ,\Phi=(1-e^{-\beta})\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-k\beta}|k\rangle\langle k|,\qquad e^{-\beta}=\frac{1-\mu}{\mu},

which has centered Gaussian distributions for both 𝐐{\bf Q} and 𝐏{\bf P} with variance 1/(4​μ−2)>1/21/(4\mu-2)>1/2. We define a family of displaced thermal equilibrium states

Φζ:=Dζ​(Φ):=W⁡(ζ/2​μ−1)​Φ​W​(ζ/2​μ−1)∗,\Phi^{\zeta}:=D^{\zeta}(\Phi):=W(\zeta/\sqrt{2\mu-1})\,\Phi\,W(\zeta/\sqrt{2\mu-1})^{*}, (1.3)

where W⁡(ζ):=exp⁡(ζ​a∗−ζ​a)W(\zeta):=\exp(\zeta a^{*}-\zeta a) is the unitary displacement operator with ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C}. Additionally we consider a classical Gaussian shift model consisting of the family of normal distributions N⁡(u,μ⁡(1−μ))N(u,\mu(1-\mu)) with unknown center uu and fixed known variance. The classical-quantum statistical experiment to which we alluded above is

ℛ:={Φθ:=N⁡(u,μ⁡(1−μ))⊗Φζ:‖θ‖≤C}\mathcal{R}:=\{\Phi^{\theta}:=N(u,\mu(1-\mu))\otimes\Phi^{\zeta}:\|\theta\|\leq C\} (1.4)

where the unknown parameters θ=(u,ζ)∈ℝ×ℂ\theta=(u,\zeta)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{C} are the same as those of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}.

Theorem 1.1.

[18, 15] Let 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} be the quantum statistical experiment (1.2) and let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the classical-quantum experiment (1.4). Then for each nn there exist quantum channels (normalized completely positive maps)

Tn\displaystyle T_{n} :\displaystyle: M⁡((ℂ2)⊗n)→L1​(ℝ)⊗𝒯⁡(L2​(ℝ)),\displaystyle M\left((\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}\right)\to L^{1}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{T}(L^{2}(\mathbb{R})),
Sn\displaystyle S_{n} :\displaystyle: L1​(ℝ)⊗𝒯⁡(L2​(ℝ))→M⁡((ℂ2)⊗n),\displaystyle L^{1}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{T}(L^{2}(\mathbb{R}))\to M\left((\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}\right),

with 𝒯​(L2​(ℝ))\mathcal{T}(L^{2}(\mathbb{R})) the trace-class operators, such that

limn→∞sup‖θ‖≤C‖Φθ−Tn​(ρθn)‖1=0,\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\,\sup_{\|\theta\|\leq C}\,\|\Phi_{\theta}-T_{n}\left(\rho^{n}_{\theta}\right)\|_{1}=0,
limn→∞sup‖θ‖≤C‖ρθn−Sn​(Φθ)‖1=0,\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\,\sup_{\|\theta\|\leq C}\,\|\rho^{n}_{\theta}-S_{n}\left(\Phi_{\theta}\right)\|_{1}=0,

for an arbitrary constant C>0C>0.

The theorem shows that from a statistical point of view the joint qubits states are asymptotically indistinguishable from the limit Gaussian system. At the first sight one might object that the local nature of the result prevents us from drawing any conclusions for the original model of a completely unknown state ρ\rho. However this is not a limitation, but reflects the correct normalisation of the parameters with n→∞n\to\infty. Indeed as nn grows we have more information about the state which can be pinned down to a region of size slightly larger that 1/n1/\sqrt{n} by performing rough measurements on a small proportion of the systems. After this ‘localisation’ step, we can use more sophisticated techniques to better estimate the state within the local neighborhood of the first step estimator, and it is here where we use the local asymptotic normality result. Indeed, since locally the states are uniformly close to displaced Gaussian states we can pull back the optimal (heterodyne) measurement for estimating the latter to get an asymptotically optimal measurement for the former. Based on this insight we have proposed a realistic measurement set-up for this purpose using an atom-field interaction and continuous measurements in the field [15].

This paper deals with the extension of the previous result to dd-dimensional systems. Like in the two-dimensional case we parametrise the neighbourhood of a fixed (diagonal) state ρ0\rho_{0} by a vector u→∈ℝd−1\vec{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1} of diagonal parameters and d⁡(d−1)/2d(d-1)/2 complex parameters ζ→=(ζj,k:j<k)\vec{\zeta}=(\zeta_{j,k}:j<k), one for each off-diagonal matrix element (cf. (4.2) and (4.4)). We consider the same 1/n−1/\sqrt{n}-scaling and look at the family

𝒬n={[ρθ/n]⊗n:θ=(u→,ζ→)∈Θn⊂ℝd−1⊗ℂd⁡(d−1)/2},\mathcal{Q}_{n}=\left\{\left[\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}\right]^{\otimes n}:\theta=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta})\in\Theta_{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2}\right\},

where Θn\Theta_{n} is a ball of local parameters whose size is allowed to grow slowly with nn.

As in the 22-dimensional case, the limit model is the product of a classical statistical model depending on the parameters u→\vec{u} and a quantum model depending on ζ→\vec{\zeta}. Moreover the quantum part splits into a tensor product of displaced thermal states of quantum oscillators, one for each off-diagonal matrix element ζj,k\zeta_{j,k} with j<kj<k. Thus

Φθ=N⁡(u→,Iρ0−1)⊗⨂j<kΦj,kζj,k,θ=(u→,ζ→).\Phi^{\theta}=N(\vec{u},I_{\rho_{0}}^{-1})\otimes\bigotimes_{j<k}\Phi^{\zeta_{j,k}}_{j,k},\qquad\theta=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta}).

Here, Iρ0I_{\rho_{0}} is the Fisher information matrix of the multinomial model with parameters (μ1,…,μd)(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}) described in Example 3.5, and Φj,kζj,k\Phi^{\zeta_{j,k}}_{j,k} is the displaced thermal equilibrium state defined in (4.35) with inverse temperature β=ln⁡(μj/μk)\beta=\ln(\mu_{j}/\mu_{k}).

Theorem 4.3 is the main result of the paper and shows the convergence of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} to the Gaussian model

ℛn={Φθ:θ∈Θn⊂ℝd−1⊗ℂd⁡(d−1)/2},\mathcal{R}_{n}=\left\{\Phi^{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2}\right\},

in the spirit of Theorem 1.1. On the technical side, the uniform convergence holds over local neighbourhoods Θn\Theta_{n} which are allowed to grow with nn rather that being fixed balls. This is essential for constructing the two stage optimal measurement: first localise within a neighbourhood Θn\Theta_{n}, and then apply the optimal Gaussian measurement. The details of this construction are similar to the two dimensional case and will be given in a subsequent paper [17].

Despite the similarity to the two dimensional case, the proof of the dd-dimensional result has additional features which may be responsible for the fact that the optimal estimation problem has remained unsolved until now. The proof is based on the following observations:

  • •

    the nn systems space (ℂd)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} decomposes into a direct sum of irreducible representations of S​U​(d)SU(d), each representation being labelled by a Young diagram λ\lambda (cf. Theorem 4.1);

  • •

    the joint state ρθ/n⊗n\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}^{\otimes n} has the block diagonal form (4.8), the block weights λ→pλθ,n\lambda\to p^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} depend only on the diagonal parameters u→\vec{u} and are closely related to the multinomial distribution of Example 3.5. This classical statistical model converges to the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Gaussian shift model N⁡(u→,Iρ0−1)N(\vec{u},I^{-1}_{\rho_{0}});

  • •

    there exists an isometry VλV_{\lambda} mapping basis vectors |𝐦,λ⟩\left|{\bf m},\lambda\right\rangle of the irreducible representation ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} almost into number vectors |𝐦⟩\left|{\bf m}\right\rangle of the multimode Fock space, where 𝐦={mj,k:j<k}{\bf m}=\{m_{j,k}:j<k\} is the collection of number eigenvalues for all oscillators.

  • •

    given a typical λ\lambda, the conditional block-state ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} can be mapped with VλV_{\lambda} into a multimode state which is close (in trace norm) to the Gaussian product state ⊗j<kΦj,kζj,k\otimes_{j<k}\Phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}}. This can be done uniformly over the typical diagrams whose normalised shapes have 1/n1/\sqrt{n} fluctuations around (μ1,μ2,…,μd)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\dots,\mu_{d}), and over parameters θ∈Θn\theta\in\Theta_{n}.

The first item is the well known Weyl duality which is extensively used in quantum statistics for i.i.d. states. The probability distribution of the second point has also been analysed the context of large deviations [30] for the estimation of the state eigenvalues. The third point shows that the basis |𝐦,λ⟩|{\bf m},\lambda\rangle is almost orthogonal for indices 𝐦{\bf m} which are not too big. This basis is obtained by projecting tensors of the form f𝐚:=fa⁡(1)⊗⋯⊗fa⁡(n)f_{\bf a}:=f_{a(1)}\otimes\dots\otimes f_{a(n)} onto a subspace of (ℂd)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} which is isomorphic to ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} (cf. Theorem 5.2). Let us place the indices {a⁡(i):i=1​…​n}\{a(i):i=1\dots n\} in the boxes of the diagram λ\lambda along rows, starting from the left end of the first row, to obtain a tableau t𝐚t_{\bf a}. It turns out that we only need to consider f𝐚f_{\bf a} for which t𝐚t_{\bf a} is a semistandard tableau (nondecreasing along rows, increasing along columns). The relatively large number of ii’s in the row ii is intentional, since it turns out that the ‘relevant’ vectors, i.e. those carrying the states ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}, have indices mi,jm_{i,j} small compared with the length of the rows (λi≈n​μi\lambda_{i}\approx n\mu_{i} for typical representations λ\lambda). More precisely, in section 7.2 we prove the following quasi-orthogonality result which allows us to carry the block states over to the oscillator space: if 𝐦≠𝐥{\bf m}\neq{\bf l} and |𝐥|≤|𝐦|≤nη|{\bf l}|\leq|{\bf m}|\leq n^{\eta} then

|⟨𝐦,λ|𝐥,λ⟩|=O(n(9​η−2)​|𝐦−𝐥|/12)→n→∞0forη<2/9.|\langle{\bf m},\lambda|{\bf l},\lambda\rangle|=O(n^{(9\eta-2)|{\bf m}-{\bf l}|/12})\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0\qquad{\rm for~}\eta<2/9.

The proof of the fourth point involves a detailed analysis of the state ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} through its coefficients in the basis |𝐦,λ⟩\left|{\bf m},\lambda\right\rangle of ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}. When θ=0\theta=0 the state is diagonal and its coefficients approach uniformly those of the multidimensional thermal state Φ0→=⊗j<kΦj,k\Phi^{\vec{0}}=\otimes_{j<k}\Phi_{j,k} as shown in Lemma 6.3. The next step is to apply S​U​(d)SU(d) rotations and obtain the states ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}. In Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5 it is shown that the unitary operations Ad​[Uλ​(ζ/n)]{\rm Ad}[U_{\lambda}(\zeta/\sqrt{n})] act on ρλ0,n\rho^{0,n}_{\lambda} in the same way as the displacement operator Dζ→D^{\vec{\zeta}} acts on the thermal state Φ0→\Phi^{\vec{0}}. A remarkable fact is that in the limit the different off-diagonal parameters ‘separate’ into a product of shift experiments for quantum oscillators, one for each off-diagonal index (j<k)(j<k). This could be guessed from the Quantum Central Limit Theorem 4.4 which is related to the restriction of our result to θ=0\theta=0.

Due to the apparent intricacy of the main result, the paper is organised according to the ‘onion peeling’ principle. We start in section 2 with general classical statistical notions which motivate our investigation in quantum statistics. In particular we explain the relevance of the Le Cam distance between statistical models as a statistically meaningful way to describe convergence. Section 3 presents the classical version of local asymptotic normality with the multinomial model as example.

In section 4 we introduce the quantum statistical model consisting of nn identical quantum systems with joint state ρθ,n\rho^{\theta,n} described by diagonal and rotation parameters. We also introduce the multimode Gaussian states appearing in the limit. With this we can formulate the main result, Theorem 4.3.

In section 5 we introduce the basis |𝐦,λ⟩|{\bf m},\lambda\rangle and the isometry VλV_{\lambda} allowing us to define the channels TnT_{n} and SnS_{n} connecting the two statistical models.

In section 6 we break the proof of the main theorem into manageable lemmas, essentially by using triangle inequalities. Each lemma deals with a different aspect of the convergence and has an interest in its own.

Finally, the technical proofs are collected in section 7. Notably, subsection 7.1 and Lemma 7.1 contain the combinatorial substance of the paper.

Our investigation relies on the theory of representations of S​U​(d)SU(d). We refer to [10, 14, 11] for proofs of standard results and more details.

As in the two-dimensional case [15], local asymptotic normality provides a two stage adaptive measurement strategy which is asymptotically optimal for both Bayesian and pointwise viewpoints, and for a large range of ‘distances’ on the state space [17].

2 Classical and quantum statistical experiments

In this section we introduce some basic notions from classical statistics with the aim of defining the Le Cam distance between statistical models and local asymptotic normality. In parallel, we will define the quantum analogues and point out their relevance in quantum statistics. The reader may find the conceptual framework helpful in understanding the quantum version of the result, but otherwise the section can be skipped at the first reading.

Let XX be a random variable with values in the measure space (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}), and let us assume that its probability distribution PP belongs to some family {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} where the parameter θ\theta is unknown. Statistical inference deals with the question of how to use the available data XX in order to draw conclusions about some property of θ\theta. We shall call the family

ℰ:={Pθ:θ∈Θ},\mathcal{E}:=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}, (2.1)

a statistical experiment or statistical model over (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}) [31].

In quantum statistics the data is replaced by a quantum system prepared in a state ϕ\phi which belongs to a family {ϕθ:θ∈Θ}\{\phi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} of states over an algebra of observables. In order to make a statistical inference about θ\theta one first has to measure the system, and then apply statistical techniques to draw conclusions from the data consisting of the measurement outcomes. An important difference with the classical case is that the experimenter has the possibility to choose the measurement set-up MM, and each set-up will lead to a different classical model {Pθ(M):θ∈Θ}\{P^{(M)}_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}, where Pθ(M)P^{(M)}_{\theta} is the distribution of outcomes when performing the measurement MM on the system prepared in state ϕθ\phi_{\theta}.

The guiding idea of this paper is to investigate the structure of the family of quantum states

𝒬:={ϕθ:θ∈Θ},\mathcal{Q}:=\{\phi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\},

which will be called a quantum statistical experiment. We shall show that in an important asymptotic set-up, namely that of a large number of identically prepared systems, the joint state can be approximated by a multidimensional quantum Gaussian state, for all possible preparations of the individual systems. This will bring a drastic simplification in the problem of optimal estimation for dd-dimensional quantum systems, which can then be solved in the asymptotic framework [17].

2.1 Classical and quantum randomizations

Any statistical decision (e.g. estimator, test) can be seen as data processing using a Markov kernel. Suppose we are given a random variable XX taking values in (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}) and we want to produce a ‘decision’ y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} based on the data XX. The space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} may be for example the parameter space Θ\Theta in the case of estimation, or just the set {0,1}\{0,1\} in the case of testing between two hypotheses. For every value x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} we choose yy randomly with probability distribution given by Kx​(d​y)K_{x}(dy). Assuming that K:𝒳×Σ𝒴→[0,1]K:\mathcal{X}\times\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}\to[0,1] is measurable with respect to xx for all fixed A∈Σ𝒴A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}, we can regard KK as a map from probability distributions over (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}) to probability distributions over (𝒴,Σ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}) with

K⁡(P)​(A)=∫Kx​(A)​P​(𝑑x),A∈Σ𝒴.K(P)(A)=\int K_{x}(A)P(dx),\quad A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}. (2.2)

A statistic S:𝒳→𝒴S:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} is a particular example of such a procedure, where KxK_{x} is simply the delta measure at S⁡(x)S(x).

Besides statistical decisions, there is another important reason why one would like to apply such treatment to the data, namely to summarize it in a more convenient and informative way for future purposes as illustrated in the following simple example. Consider nn independent identically distributed random variables X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} with values in {0,1}\{0,1\} and distribution Pθ:=(1−θ,θ)P_{\theta}:=(1-\theta,\theta) with θ∈Θ:=(0,1)\theta\in\Theta:=(0,1). The associated statistical experiment is

ℰn:={Pθn:θ∈Θ}.\mathcal{E}_{n}:=\{P_{\theta}^{n}:\theta\in\Theta\}.

It is easy to see that X¯n=1n​∑i=1nXi\bar{X}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i} is an unbiased estimator of θ\theta and moreover it is a sufficient statistic for ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}, i.e. the conditional distribution Pθn(⋅|X¯n=x¯)P_{\theta}^{n}(\cdot|\bar{X}_{n}=\bar{x}) does not depend on θ\theta! In other words the dependence on θ\theta of the total sample (X1,X2,…,Xn)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) is completely captured by the statistic X¯n\bar{X}_{n} which can be used as such for any statistical decision problem concerning ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}. If we denote by P¯θn\bar{P}^{n}_{\theta} the distribution of X¯n\bar{X}_{n} then the experiment

ℰ¯n={P¯θn:θ∈Θ},\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{n}=\{\bar{P}^{n}_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\},

is statistically equivalent to ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}. To convince ourselves that X¯n\bar{X}_{n} does contain the same statistical information as (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}), we show that we can obtain the latter from the former by means of a randomized statistic. Indeed for every fixed value x¯\bar{x} of X¯n\bar{X}_{n} there exists a measurable function

fx¯:[0,1]→{0,1}n,f_{\bar{x}}:[0,1]\to\{0,1\}^{n},

such that the distribution of fx¯​(U)f_{\bar{x}}(U) is Pθn(⋅|X¯n=x¯)P^{n}_{\theta}(\cdot|\bar{X}_{n}=\bar{x}). In other words

λ⁡(fx¯−1​(x1,…,xn))=Pθn​(x1,…,xn|X¯n=x¯),\lambda(f_{\bar{x}}^{-1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))=P^{n}_{\theta}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}|\bar{X}_{n}=\bar{x}),

where λ\lambda is the Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1]. Then F⁡(X¯n,U):=fX¯n​(U),F(\bar{X}_{n},U):=f_{\bar{X}_{n}}(U), has distribution PθnP_{\theta}^{n}. To summarize, statistics, randomized statistics and Markov kernels, are ways to transform the available data for a specific purpose. The Markov kernel KK defined in (2.2) maps the experiment ℰ\mathcal{E} of equation (2.1) into the experiment

ℱ:={Qθ:θ∈Θ},\mathcal{F}:=\{Q_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\},

over (𝒴,Σ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}) with Qθ=K⁡(Pθ)Q_{\theta}=K(P_{\theta}). For mathematical convenience it is useful to represent such transformations in terms of linear maps between linear spaces.

Definition 2.1.

A positive linear map

T∗:L1​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→L1​(𝒴,Σ𝒴,Q)T_{*}:L^{1}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to L^{1}(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},Q)

is called a stochastic operator or transition if ‖T∗​(g)‖1=‖g‖1\|T_{*}(g)\|_{1}=\|g\|_{1} for every g∈L+1​(𝒳)g\in L_{+}^{1}(\mathcal{X}).

Definition 2.2.

A positive linear map

T:L∞​(𝒴,Σ𝒴,Q)→L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)T:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},Q)\to L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)

is called a Markov operator if T​𝟏=𝟏T\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}, and if for any fn↓0f_{n}\downarrow 0 in L∞​(𝒴)L^{\infty}(\mathcal{Y}) we have T​fn↓0Tf_{n}\downarrow 0.

A pair (T∗,T)(T_{*},T) as above is called a dual pair if

∫f​T​(g)​𝑑P=∫T∗​(f)​g​𝑑Q,\int fT(g)dP=\int T_{*}(f)gdQ,

for all f∈L1​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)f\in L^{1}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P) and g∈L∞​(𝒴,Σ𝒴,Q)g\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},Q). It is a theorem that for any stochastic operator T∗T_{*} there exists a unique dual Markov operator TT and vice versa.

What is the relation between Markov operators and Markov kernels ? Roughly speaking, any Markov kernel defines a Markov operator when we restrict to families of dominated probability measures. Let us assume that all distributions PθP_{\theta} of the experiment ℰ\mathcal{E} defined in (2.1) are absolutely continuous with respect to a fixed probability distribution PP, such that there exist densities pθ:=d​Pθ/d​P:𝒳→ℝ+p_{\theta}:=dP_{\theta}/dP:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}. Such an experiment is called dominated and in concrete situations this condition is usually satisfied. Let Kx​(d​y)K_{x}(dy) be a Markov kernel (2.2) such that Qθ=K⁡(Pθ)Q_{\theta}=K(P_{\theta}), then we define associated Markov operator (T⁡(f))​(x):=∫f⁡(y)​kx​(𝑑y)(T(f))(x):=\int f(y)k_{x}(dy) and have

Qθ=Pθ∘T,∀θ.Q_{\theta}=P_{\theta}\circ T,\qquad\forall\theta. (2.3)

When the probability distributions of two experiments are related to each other as in (2.3), we say that ℱ\mathcal{F} is a randomization of ℰ\mathcal{E}. From the duality between TT and T∗T_{*} we obtain an equivalent characterization in terms of the stochastic operator T∗:L1​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→L1​(𝒴,Σ𝒴,Q)T_{*}:L^{1}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to L^{1}(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},Q) such that

T∗​(d​Pθ/d​P)=d​Qθ/d​Q,∀θ.T_{*}(dP_{\theta}/dP)=dQ_{\theta}/dQ,\qquad\forall\theta\,.

The concept of randomization is weaker than that of Markov kernel transformation, but under the additional condition that (𝒴,Σ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}) is locally compact space with countable base and Borel σ\sigma-field, it can be shown that any randomization can be implemented by a Markov kernel [41].

What is the analogue of randomizations in the quantum case ? In the language of operator algebras L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P) is a commutative von Neumann algebra and L1​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)L^{1}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P) is the space of (densities of) normal linear functionals on it. The stochastic operator T∗T_{*} is the classical version of quantum channel, i.e. a completely positive normalized (trace-preserving) map

T∗:𝒜∗→ℬ∗T_{*}:\mathcal{A}_{*}\to\mathcal{B}_{*}

where 𝒜∗,ℬ∗\mathcal{A}_{*},\mathcal{B}_{*} are the spaces of normal states on the von Neumann algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} and respectively ℬ\mathcal{B}. Any normal state ϕ\phi on 𝒜\mathcal{A} has a density ρ\rho with respect to the trace such that ϕ⁡(A)=Tr⁡(ρ​A)\phi(A)=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho A) for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}. The dual of T∗T_{*} is

T:ℬ→𝒜,T:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A},

which is a unital completely positive map and has the property that T∗​(ϕ)​(b)=ϕ⁡(T⁡(b))T_{*}(\phi)(b)=\phi(T(b)) for all b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B} and ϕ∈𝒜∗\phi\in\mathcal{A}_{*}. We interpret such quantum channels as possible physical transformations from input to output states.

A particular class of channels is that of measurements. In this case the input is the state of a quantum system described by an algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and the output is a probability distribution over the space of outcomes (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}). Any measurement is described by a positive linear map

M:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→𝒜,M:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{A},

which is completely specified by the image of characteristic functions of measurable sets, also called positive operator valued measure (POVM). This map M:Σ𝒳→𝒜M:\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathcal{A} has following properties

  1. 1.

    Positive: M⁡(A)≥0,∀A∈Σ𝒳M(A)\geq 0,\qquad\forall\,A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}} ;

  2. 2.

    Countably additive: ∑i=1∞M(Ai)=M(∪iAi),Ai∩Aj=∅,i≠j\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}M(A_{i})=M(\cup_{i}A_{i}),\quad A_{i}\cap A_{j}=\emptyset,i\neq j;

  3. 3.

    Normalized: M⁡(𝒳)=𝟏M(\mathcal{X})=\mathbf{1}.

The corresponding channel acting on states is a positive map M∗:𝒜∗→L1​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)M_{*}:\mathcal{A}_{*}\to L^{1}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P) given by

M⁡(ϕ)​(A)=ϕ⁡(M⁡(A))=Tr⁡(ρ​M​(A)),M(\phi)(A)=\phi(M(A))=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho M(A)),

where ρ\rho is the density matrix of ϕ\phi. By applying the channel MM to the quantum statistical experiment consisting of the family of states 𝒬=(ϕθ:θ∈Θ)\mathcal{Q}=(\phi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta) on 𝒜\mathcal{A} we obtain a classical statistical experiment

𝒬M:={M⁡(ϕθ):θ∈Θ},\mathcal{Q}_{M}:=\{M(\phi_{\theta}):\theta\in\Theta\},

over the outcomes space (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}).

As in the classical case, quantum channels can be seen as ways to compare quantum experiments. The first steps in this direction were made by Petz [36, 38, 34] who developed the theory of quantum sufficiency dealing with the problem of characterizing when a sub-algebra of observables contains the same statistical information about a family of states, as the original algebra. More generally, two experiments 𝒬:={𝒜,ϕθ:θ∈Θ}\mathcal{Q}:=\{\mathcal{A},\phi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} and ℛ:={ℬ,ψθ:θ∈Θ}\mathcal{R}:=\{\mathcal{B},\psi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} are called statistically equivalent if there exist channels T:𝒜→ℬT:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B} and S:ℬ→𝒜S:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A} such that

ψθ∘T=ϕθandϕθ∘S=ψθ∀θ.\psi_{\theta}\circ T=\phi_{\theta}\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\phi_{\theta}\circ S=\psi_{\theta}\qquad\forall\theta.

As consequence, for any measurement M:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→𝒜M:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{A} there exists a measurement T∘M:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→ℬT\circ M:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{B} such that the resulting classical experiments coincide 𝒬M=ℛT∘M\mathcal{Q}_{M}=\mathcal{R}_{T\circ M}. Thus for any statistical problem, and any procedure concerning the experiment 𝒬\mathcal{Q} there exists a procedure for ℛ\mathcal{R} with the same risk (average cost), and vice versa.

2.2 The Le Cam distance and its statistical meaning

We have seen that two experiments are statistically equivalent when they can be transformed into each other be means of quantum channels. When this cannot be done exactly, we would like to have a measure of how close the two experiments are when we allow any channel transformation. We define the deficiency of ℛ\mathcal{R} with respect to 𝒬\mathcal{Q} as

δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)=infTsupθ‖ϕθ−ψθ∘T‖\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})=\inf_{T}\sup_{\theta}\|\phi_{\theta}-\psi_{\theta}\circ T\| (2.4)

where the infimum is taken over all channels T:𝒜→ℬT:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}. The norm distance between two states on 𝒜\mathcal{A} is defined as

∥ϕ1−ϕ2∥:=sup{|ϕ1(a)−ϕ2(a)|:a∈𝒜,∥a∥≤1},\|\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}\|:=\,\sup\{|\phi_{1}(a)-\phi_{2}(a)|:a\in\mathcal{A},\|a\|\leq 1\},

and for 𝒜=ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) it is equal to ‖ρ1−ρ2‖1:=Tr⁡(|ρ1−ρ2|)\|\rho_{1}-\rho_{2}\|_{1}:=\mathrm{Tr}(|\rho_{1}-\rho_{2}|), where ρi\rho_{i} is the density matrix of the state ϕi\phi_{i}. When δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)=0\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})=0 we say that ℛ\mathcal{R} is more informative than 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Note that δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q}) is not symmetric but satisfies a triangle inequality of the form δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)+δ⁡(𝒬,𝒯)≥δ⁡(ℛ,𝒯)\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})+\delta(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{T})\geq\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{T}). By symmetrizing we obtain a proper distance over the space of equivalence classes of experiments, called Le Cam’s distance [31]

Δ⁡(𝒬,ℛ):=max⁡(δ⁡(𝒬,ℛ),δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)).\Delta(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}):=\rm{max}\left(\delta(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R})\,,\,\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})\right). (2.5)

What is the statistical meaning of the Le Cam distance ? We shall show that if δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)≤ϵ\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})\leq\epsilon then for any statistical decision problem with loss function between 00 and 11, any measurement procedure for 𝒬\mathcal{Q} can be matched by a measurement procedure for ℛ\mathcal{R} whose risk will be at most ϵ\epsilon larger than the previous one.

A decision problem is specified by a decision space (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}) and a loss function Wθ:𝒳→[0,1]W_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] for each θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. We are given a quantum system prepared in the state ϕθ∈𝒜∗\phi_{\theta}\in\mathcal{A}_{*} with unknown parameter θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta and would like to perform a measurement with outcomes in 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that the expected value of the loss function WθW_{\theta} is small. Let

M:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→𝒜,M:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{A},

be such a measurement, and Pθ(M)=ϕθ∘MP^{(M)}_{\theta}=\phi_{\theta}\circ M, then the risk at θ\theta is

R⁡(M,θ):=∫𝒳Wθ​(x)​Pθ(M)​(𝑑x).R(M,\theta):=\int_{\mathcal{X}}W_{\theta}(x)P^{(M)}_{\theta}(dx).

Since the point θ\theta is unknown one would like to obtain a small risk over all possible realizations

Rm​a​x​(M)=supθ∈ΘR⁡(M,θ).R_{max}(M)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(M,\theta).

The minimax risk is then Rm​i​n​m​a​x:=infMRm​a​x​(M)R_{minmax}:=\inf_{M}R_{max}(M). In the Bayesian framework one considers a prior distribution π\pi over Θ\Theta and then averages the risk with respect to π\pi

Rπ​(M)=∫ΘR⁡(M,θ)​π​(𝑑θ).R_{\pi}(M)=\int_{\Theta}R(M,\theta)\pi(d\theta).

The optimal risk in this case is Rπ:=infMRπ​(M)R_{\pi}:=\inf_{M}R_{\pi}(M).

Coming back to the experiments 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and ℛ\mathcal{R} we shall compare their achievable risks for a given decision problem as above. Consider the measurement N:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→ℬN:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{B} given by N=T∘MN=T\circ M where T:𝒜→ℬT:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B} is the channel which achieves the infimum in (2.4). Then

R⁡(N,θ)\displaystyle R(N,\theta) =\displaystyle= ∫𝒳W⁡(θ,x)​Pθ(N)​(𝑑x)=ψθ​(T∘M⁡(Wθ))\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}}W(\theta,x)P^{(N)}_{\theta}(dx)=\psi_{\theta}(T\circ M(W_{\theta}))
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖ψθ∘T−ϕθ‖+ϕθ​(M⁡(Wθ))≤δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬)+R⁡(M,θ),\displaystyle\|\psi_{\theta}\circ T-\phi_{\theta}\|+\phi_{\theta}(M(W_{\theta}))\leq\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q})+R(M,\theta),

where we have used the fact that 0≤Wθ≤10\leq W_{\theta}\leq 1.

Lemma 2.3.

For every achievable risk R⁡(M,θ)R(M,\theta) for 𝒬\mathcal{Q} there exists a measurement N:L∞​(𝒳,Σ𝒳,P)→ℬN:L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},P)\to\mathcal{B} for ℛ\mathcal{R} such that

R⁡(N,θ)≤R⁡(M,θ)+δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬).R(N,\theta)\leq R(M,\theta)+\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q}).

In consequence

Rm​i​n​m​a​x​(ℛ)≤Rm​i​n​m​a​x​(𝒬)+δ⁡(ℛ,𝒬).R_{minmax}(\mathcal{R})\leq R_{minmax}(\mathcal{Q})+\delta(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{Q}).

3 Local asymptotic normality in statistics

In this section we describe the notion of local asymptotic normality and its significance in statistics [31, 42, 41, 43]. Suppose that we observe X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} where XiX_{i} take values in a measurable space (𝒳,Σ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}) and are are independent, identically distributed with distribution PθP_{\theta} indexed by a parameter θ\theta belonging to an open subset Θ⊂ℝm\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{m}. The full sample is a single observation from the product PθnP_{\theta}^{n} of nn copies of PθP_{\theta} on the sample space (Ωn,Σn)(\Omega^{n},\Sigma^{n}). Local asymptotic normality means that for large nn such statistical experiments can be approximated by Gaussian experiments after a suitable reparametrisation. Let θ0\theta_{0} be a fixed point and define a local parameter u=n​(θ−θ0)u=\sqrt{n}(\theta-\theta_{0}) characterizing points in a small neighbourhood of θ0\theta_{0}, and rewrite PθnP_{\theta}^{n} as Pθ0+u/nnP_{\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n}}^{n} seen as a distribution depending on the parameter uu. Local asymptotic normality means that for large nn the experiments

{Pθ0+u/nn:u∈ℝm}and{N⁡(u,Iθ0−1):u∈ℝm},\left\{P_{\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n}}^{n}:u\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\}\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\left\{N(u,I_{\theta_{0}}^{-1}):u\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\},

have the same statistical properties when the models θ↦Pθ\theta\mapsto P_{\theta} are sufficiently ‘smooth’. The point of this result is that while the original experiment may be difficult to analyse, the limit one is a tractable Gaussian shift experiment in which we observe a single sample from the normal distribution with unknown mean uu and fixed variance matrix Iθ0−1I_{\theta_{0}}^{-1}. Here

[Iθ0]i​j=𝔼θ0​[ℓθ0,i​ℓθ0,j],\left[I_{\theta_{0}}\right]_{ij}=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}}\left[\ell_{\theta_{0},i}\ell_{\theta_{0},j}\right],

is the Fisher information matrix at θ0\theta_{0}, with ℓθ,i:=∂log⁡pθ/∂θi\ell_{\theta,i}:=\partial\log p_{\theta}/\partial\theta_{i} the score function and pθp_{\theta} is the density of PθP_{\theta} with respect to a reference probability distribution PP.

There exist two formulations of the result depending on the notion of convergence which one uses. In this paper we only discuss the strong version based on convergence with respect to the Le Cam distance, and we refer to [43] for another formulation using the so called weak convergence (convergence in distribution of finite dimensional marginals of the likelihood ratio process), and to [16] for its generalization to quantum statistical experiments.

Before formulating the theorem, we explain what sufficiently smooth means. The least restrictive condition is that pθp_{\theta} is differentiable in quadratic mean, i.e. there exists a measurable function ℓθ:𝒳→ℝ\ell_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} such that as u→0u\to 0

∫[pθ+u1/2−pθ1/2−ut​ℓθ​pθ1/2]2​𝑑P→0.\int\left[p_{\theta+u}^{1/2}-p_{\theta}^{1/2}-u^{t}\ell_{\theta}p_{\theta}^{1/2}\right]^{2}dP\to 0.

Note that ℓθ\ell_{\theta} must still be interpreted as score function since under some regularity conditions we have ∂pθ1/2/∂θi=12​(∂log⁡pθ/∂θi)​pθ1/2\partial p_{\theta}^{1/2}/\partial\theta_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\partial\log p_{\theta}/\partial\theta_{i})p^{1/2}_{\theta}.

Theorem 3.1.

Let ℰ:={Pθ:θ∈Θ}\mathcal{E}:=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} be a statistical experiment with Θ⊂ℝd\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and Pθ≪PP_{\theta}\ll P such that the map θ→pθ\theta\to p_{\theta} is differentiable in quadratic mean. Define

ℰn={Pθ0+u/nn:‖u‖≤C},ℱ={N⁡(u,Iθ0−1):‖u‖≤C},\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{n}=\{P_{\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n}}^{n}:\|u\|\leq C\},\qquad\mathcal{F}=\{N(u,I_{\theta_{0}}^{-1}):\|u\|\leq C\},

with Iθ0I_{\theta_{0}} the Fisher information matrix of ℰ\mathcal{E} at point θ0\theta_{0}, and CC a positive constant. Then Δ⁡(ℰn,ℱ)→0\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{n},\mathcal{F})\to 0. In other words, there exist sequences of randomizations TnT_{n} and SnS_{n} such that:

limn→∞sup‖u‖≤C‖Tn​(Pθ0+u/nn)−N⁡(u,Iθ0−1)‖\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\,\sup_{\|u\|\leq C}\,\left\|T_{n}(P_{\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n}}^{n})-N(u,I_{\theta_{0}}^{-1})\right\| =0,\displaystyle=0,
limn→∞sup‖u‖≤C‖Pθ0+u/nn−Sn​(N⁡(u,Iθ0−1))‖\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\,\sup_{\|u\|\leq C}\,\left\|P_{\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n}}^{n}-S_{n}(N(u,I_{\theta_{0}}^{-1}))\right\| =0.\displaystyle=0.
Remark 3.2.

Note that the statement of the Theorem is not of Central Limit type which typically involves convergence in distribution to a Gaussian distribution at a single point θ0\theta_{0}. Local asymptotic normality states that the convergence is uniform around the point θ0\theta_{0}, and moreover the variance of the limit Gaussian is fixed whereas the variance obtained from the Central Limit Theorem depends on the point θ\theta. Additionally, the randomization transforming the data (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) into the Gaussian variable is the same for all θ=θ0+u/n\theta=\theta_{0}+u/\sqrt{n} and thus does not require a priori the knowledge of θ\theta.

Remark 3.3.

Local asymptotic normality is the basis of many important results in asymptotic optimality theory and explains the asymptotic normality of certain estimators such as the maximum likelihood estimator. The quantum version introduced in the next section plays a similar role for the case of quantum statistical model. An asymptotically optimal estimation strategy based on local asymptotic normality was derived in [15] for two-dimensional systems.

Remark 3.4.

Let us define the real Hilbert space L2​(θ0)=(ℝm,(⋅,⋅)θ0)L^{2}(\theta_{0})=(\mathbb{R}^{m},(\cdot,\cdot)_{\theta_{0}}) with inner product

(u,v)θ0=uT​Iθ0​v.(u,v)_{\theta_{0}}=u^{T}I_{\theta_{0}}v.

By multiplying with Iθ0I_{\theta_{0}} we see that limit experiment can be equivalently chosen to be N⁡(Iθ0​u,Iθ0)N(I_{\theta_{0}}u,I_{\theta_{0}}). The characteristic function of X∼N⁡(Iθ0​u,Iθ0)X\sim N(I_{\theta_{0}}u,I_{\theta_{0}}) is

Fu​(w):=𝔼θ0​[exp⁡(i​wT​X)]=exp⁡(−12​‖w‖θ02+i​(w,u)θ0).F_{u}(w):=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}}[\exp(iw^{T}X)]=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|w\|_{\theta_{0}}^{2}+i(w,u)_{\theta_{0}}\right). (3.1)

A similar expression will be encountered in section 4 for the case of quantum Gaussian shift experiment.

Example 3.5.

Let Pμ=(μ1,…,μd)P_{\mu}=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}) be a probability distribution with unknown parameters (μ1,…,μd−1)∈ℝ+d−1(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d-1})\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}_{+} satisfying μi>0\mu_{i}>0 and ∑i≤d−1μi<1\sum_{i\leq d-1}\mu_{i}<1. The Fisher information at a point μ\mu is

I​(μ)i​j=∑k=1d−1μk​(δi​k​μi−1⋅δj​k​μj−1)+(1−∑l=1d−1μl)−1=δi​j​μi−1+(1−∑l=1d−1μl)−1,I(\mu)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\mu_{k}(\delta_{ik}\mu_{i}^{-1}\cdot\delta_{jk}\mu_{j}^{-1})+(1-\sum_{l=1}^{d-1}\mu_{l})^{-1}=\delta_{ij}\mu_{i}^{-1}+(1-\sum_{l=1}^{d-1}\mu_{l})^{-1}, (3.2)

and its inverse is

V​(μ)i​j:=[I​(μ)−1]i​j=δi​j​μi−μi​μj.V(\mu)_{ij}:=[I(\mu)^{-1}]_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\mu_{i}-\mu_{i}\mu_{j}. (3.3)

Thus the limit experiment in this case is ℱ:=(N(u,V(μ)):u∈ℝd−1,∥u∥≤C)\mathcal{F}:=(N(u,V(\mu)):u\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1},\|u\|\leq C).

This experiment will appear again in Theorem 4.3, as the classical part of the limit Gaussian shift experiment.

4 Local asymptotic normality in quantum statistics

In this section we present the main result of the paper. Local asymptotic normality for dd-dimensional quantum systems means roughly the following: the sequence 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} of experiments consisting of joint states ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n} of nn identical quantum systems prepared independently in the same state ρ\rho, converges to a limit experiment ℛ\mathcal{R} which is a quantum-classical Gaussian model involving displaced thermal equilibrium states of d⁡(d−1)/2d(d-1)/2 oscillators and a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional classical Gaussian shift model. As in the classical case, the result has a local nature reflecting the 1/n1/\sqrt{n} rate of convergence of state estimation. A neighbourhood of a fixed diagonal state ρ0=Diag⁡(μ1,…,μd)\rho_{0}={\rm Diag}(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}) is parametrised by (changes in the) diagonal parameters u→∈ℝd−1\vec{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1} and off-diagonal parameters ζ→∈ℂd⁡(d−1)/2\vec{\zeta}\in\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2}. The latter can be implemented by small unitary rotations. The limit Gaussian model has a classical part N⁡(u→,V⁡(μ))N(\vec{u},V(\mu)) with fixed known variance V⁡(μ)V(\mu), and a quantum part ⊗j<kΦj,kζj,k\otimes_{j<k}\Phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}} with each Φj,kζj,k\Phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}} being a thermal equilibrium state with βj,k=ln⁡(μj/μk)\beta_{j,k}=\ln(\mu_{j}/\mu_{k}), displaced in phase space by an amount proportional to ζj,k\zeta_{j,k}.

The reason for choosing the above parametrisation is twofold. Firstly, it unveils the important separation between ’classical’ and ’quantum’ parameters, and the further separation among the different off-diagonal parameters. Secondly, it is very convenient for the proof. However as we will see in ???, the limit experiment can be formulated in a ‘coordinate-free’ way in terms of quasifree states on C​C​RCCR-algebra. Although it is not needed in the main theorem, we include this formulation linking our result to the Quantum Central Limit Theorem. We stress again that local asymptotic normality is not a consequence of the Central Limit Theorem, indeed the latter is not even an ingredient in the proof but gives an indication as to what is the limit state when all parameters are zero.

4.1 The nn-tuple of dd-dimensional systems

As explained in section 3 for the classical case, our theory will be local in nature, so we will be interested in a (shrinking) neighbourhood of an arbitrary but fixed faithful state

ρ0=[μ10…00μ2⋱⋱⋱00…0μd]with​μ1>μ2>⋯>μd>0,\rho_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}\mu_{1}&0&\dots&0\\ 0&\mu_{2}&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\ 0&\dots&0&\mu_{d}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\qquad\mathrm{with}\ \mu_{1}>\mu_{2}>\dots>\mu_{d}>0, (4.1)

which for technical reasons is chosen to have different eigenvalues. A sufficiently small neighbourhood of ρ0\rho_{0} in the state space can be parametrised by θ:=(u→,ζ→)\theta:=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta}) as follows

ρ~θ:=[μ1+u1ζ1,2∗…ζ1,d∗ζ1,2μ2+u2⋱⋱⋱ζd−1,d∗ζ1,d…ζd−1,dμd−∑i=1d−1ui],ui∈ℝ,ζj,k∈ℂ.\tilde{\rho}_{\theta}:=\begin{bmatrix}\mu_{1}+u_{1}&\zeta_{1,2}^{*}&\dots&\zeta_{1,d}^{*}\\ \zeta_{1,2}&\mu_{2}+u_{2}&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\zeta_{d-1,d}^{*}\\ \zeta_{1,d}&\dots&\zeta_{d-1,d}&\mu_{d}-\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}u_{i}\end{bmatrix},\qquad u_{i}\in\mathbb{R},~\zeta_{j,k}\in\mathbb{C}. (4.2)

Indeed, note that if θ\theta is small enough then ρ~θ\tilde{\rho}_{\theta} is a density matrix.

Let δ:=inf1≤i≤dμi−μi+1\delta:=\inf_{1\leq i\leq d}\mu_{i}-\mu_{i+1}, with μd+1=0\mu_{d+1}=0, be the separation between the eigenvalues. In the first order in θ/δ\theta/\sqrt{\delta}, the family ρ~θ\tilde{\rho}_{\theta} is obtained by first perturbing the diagonal elements of ρ0\rho_{0} with u→\vec{u} and then performing a small unitary transformation with

U⁡(ζ→):=exp⁡[i⁡(∑1≤j<k≤dRe⁡(ζj,k)​Tj,k+Im⁡(ζj,k)​Tk,jμj−μk)]U(\vec{\zeta}):=\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq d}\frac{{\rm Re}(\zeta_{j,k})T_{j,k}+{\rm Im}(\zeta_{j,k})T_{k,j}}{\sqrt{\mu_{j}-\mu_{k}}}\right)\right]\\ (4.3)

where Tj,kT_{j,k} are generators of the Lie algebra of S​U​(d)SU(d) defined in (7.2). The advantage of the latter parametrisation is that we can fully exploit the machinery of irreducible group representations. For this reason, in all subsequent computations we will work with the ‘unitary’ family

ρθ:=U⁡(ζ→)​[μ1+u10…00μ2+u2⋱⋱⋱00…0μd−∑i=1d−1ui]​U∗​(ζ→),ui∈ℝ,ζj,k∈ℂ.\rho_{\theta}:=U(\vec{\zeta})\begin{bmatrix}\mu_{1}+u_{1}&0&\dots&0\\ 0&\mu_{2}+u_{2}&\ddots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\ 0&\dots&0&\mu_{d}-\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}u_{i}\end{bmatrix}U^{*}(\vec{\zeta}),\qquad u_{i}\in\mathbb{R},~\zeta_{j,k}\in\mathbb{C}. (4.4)

but we keep in mind the relationship with (4.2).

As in the classical case, the parameter θ\theta will be scaled by the factor 1/n1/\sqrt{n} meaning that we zoom in around ρ0\rho_{0} with the rate equal to the typical estimation rate based on nn samples. Let ρθ,n:=ρθ/n⊗n\rho^{\theta,n}:=\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}^{\otimes n} and let 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} be the sequence of statistical experiments

𝒬n:={ρθ,n:θ∈Θn},\mathcal{Q}_{n}:=\left\{\rho^{\theta,n}:\theta\in\Theta_{n}\right\}, (4.5)

consisting of nn systems, each one prepared in a state ρθ/n\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}} situated in a local neighborhood of ρ0\rho_{0}. The local parameter θ=(u→,ζ→)\theta=(\overrightarrow{u},\overrightarrow{\zeta}) belongs to a neighborhood Θn\Theta_{n} of the origin of ℝd−1×ℂd⁡(d−1)/2\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2} which is allowed to grow slowly with nn in a way that will be made precise later.

One of the principal tools in our result is the representation theory of the special unitary group S​U​(d)SU(d). Due to lack of space we shall not include any proofs and refer to [10, 14, 11] for details. In particular we will be working with the well known tensor representation which will be analysed in increasing depth across the following sections.

The space (ℂd)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} carries two commuting group representations: that of S​U​(d)SU(d) given by

πn​(U):|ψ1⟩⊗⋯⊗|ψn⟩↦U⁡|ψ1⟩⊗⋯⊗U⁡|ψn⟩,U∈S​U​(d),\pi_{n}(U):|\psi_{1}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes|\psi_{n}\rangle\mapsto U|\psi_{1}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes U|\psi_{n}\rangle,\qquad U\in SU(d), (4.6)

and that of the permutation group S⁡(n)S(n) given by

π~d​(τ):|ψ1⟩⊗⋯⊗|ψn⟩↦|ψτ−1​(1)⟩⊗⋯⊗|ψτ−1​(n)⟩,τ∈S⁡(n).\tilde{\pi}_{d}(\tau):|\psi_{1}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes|\psi_{n}\rangle\mapsto|\psi_{\tau^{-1}(1)}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes|\psi_{\tau^{-1}(n)}\rangle,\qquad\tau\in S(n). (4.7)

Since the two group representations commute with each other, the representation space decomposes into a direct sum of tensor products of irreducible representations. It turns out that the irreducible representations of S​U​(d)SU(d) and S⁡(n)S(n) are indexed by Young diagrams with dd rows for the former and nn boxes for the latter. A Young diagram is defined by a tuple of ordered integers λ=(λ1≥λ2​⋯≥λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\dots\geq\lambda_{k}) with λi\lambda_{i} the number of boxes on row ii (see Figure 1).

As we shall see later this pictorial representation will be very useful in understanding the structure of the irreducible representations (ℋλ,πλ)(\mathcal{H}_{\lambda},\pi_{\lambda}) of S​U​(d)SU(d).

The following theorem called Schur-Weyl duality shows that the only tensor products appearing in the above mentioned direct sum are those of irreducible representations indexed by the same λ\lambda, and in particular the algebras generated by πn​(u)\pi_{n}(u) and respectively π~d​(τ)\tilde{\pi}_{d}(\tau) are each other’s commutant!

Theorem 4.1.

Let πn\pi_{n} and π~d\tilde{\pi}_{d} be the representations of S​U​(d)SU(d) and respectively S⁡(n)S(n) on (ℂd)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}. Then the representation space decomposes into a direct sum of tensor products of irreducible representations of S​U​(d)SU(d) and S⁡(n)S(n) indexed by Young diagrams with dd lines and nn boxes:

(ℂd)⊗n\displaystyle(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} ≅\displaystyle\cong ⨁λℋλ⊗𝒦λ,\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{K}_{\lambda},
πn\displaystyle\pi_{n} ≡\displaystyle\equiv ⨁λπλ⊗𝟏𝒦λ,\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\lambda}\pi_{\lambda}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}},
π~d\displaystyle\tilde{\pi}_{d} ≡\displaystyle\equiv ⨁λ𝟏ℋλ⊗π~λ.\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}}\otimes\tilde{\pi}_{\lambda}.

In particular ρθ,n=ρθ/n⊗n\rho^{\theta,n}=\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}^{\otimes n} and π~d​(τ)\tilde{\pi}_{d}(\tau) commute for all τ\tau. Hence we have the block diagonal form for the joint states

ρθ,n=⨁λpλθ,n​ρλθ,n⊗𝟏𝒦λMn​(λ),\rho^{\theta,n}=\bigoplus_{\lambda}p^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\otimes\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}}}{M_{n}(\lambda)}, (4.8)

where Mn​(λ)M_{n}(\lambda) is the dimension of 𝒦λ\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}, pλθ,np^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} is a probability distribution over the Young diagrams, and ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} is a density matrix on ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}. From (4.4) and the Schur-Weyl duality, we get the expression of the block states

ρλθ,n=Uλ​(ζ→/n)​ρλu,0,n​Uλ​(ζ→/n)∗.\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}=U_{\lambda}(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n})\,\rho^{u,0,n}_{\lambda}\,U_{\lambda}(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n})^{*}. (4.9)

We interpret the decomposition (4.8) as follows: by doing a ‘which block’ measurement we obtain information about θ\theta through the probability density pλθ,np^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}. In fact it is easy to see that pλθ,np^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} does not depend on ζ→\vec{\zeta}, so it only gives information about the diagonal parameters u→\vec{u}. Later on we shall see that the model pθ,np^{\theta,n} has the same limit as the classical multinomial model described in Example 3.5. Once this information has been obtained, one still possesses a conditional quantum state ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}. It turns out that this state carries information about the rotation parameters ζ→\vec{\zeta}, and we will show that the statistical model described by the conditional state converges to a ‘purely quantum’ Gaussian shift experiment.

4.2 Displaced thermal equilibrium states of a harmonic oscillator

The ground state of a quantum harmonic oscillator or the laser state of a monochromatic light pulse are well known examples of quantum Gaussian states. Both physical systems are described by the same algebra of observables generated by the canonical ‘position’ and ‘momentum’ observables 𝐐{\bf Q} and 𝐏{\bf P} satisfying the Heisenberg commutation relation

𝐐𝐏−𝐏𝐐=i​𝟏.{\bf Q}{\bf P}-{\bf P}{\bf Q}=i\mathbf{1}. (4.10)

These observables can be represented on the Hilbert space L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) as

(𝐐​ψ)​(x)=x​ψ​(x),(𝐏​ψ)​(x)=−i​d​ψd​x​(x),ψ∈L2​(ℝ).({\bf Q}\psi)(x)=x\psi(x),\qquad({\bf P}\psi)(x)=-i\frac{d\psi}{dx}(x),\qquad\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). (4.11)

The space L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) has a special orthonormal basis {|0⟩,|1⟩,…}\{\left\lvert 0\right\rangle,\left\lvert 1\right\rangle,\dots\} with the vector |m⟩\left\lvert m\right\rangle given by

Hm(x)e−x2/2/(π2mm!)1/2,H_{m}(x)e^{-x^{2}/2}/(\sqrt{\pi}2^{m}m!)^{1/2},

where HmH_{m} are the Hermite polynomials. These are the eigenvectors of the number operator 𝐍:=12​(𝐐2+𝐏2−𝟏){\bf N}:=\frac{1}{2}({\bf Q}^{2}+{\bf P}^{2}-\mathbf{1}) counting the number of ‘excitations’ of the oscillator or the number of photons in the case of the light beam, such that 𝐍|m⟩=m|m⟩{\bf N}\left\lvert m\right\rangle=m\left\lvert m\right\rangle.

The creation and annihilation operators

𝐚∗=(𝐐−i​𝐏)/2,𝐚=(𝐐+i​𝐏)/2{\bf a}^{*}=({\bf Q}-i{\bf P})/\sqrt{2},\qquad{\bf a}=({\bf Q}+i{\bf P})/\sqrt{2}

satisfy [𝐚,𝐚∗]=𝟏[{\bf a},{\bf a}^{*}]=\mathbf{1} and act as ‘ladder’ operators on the basis ψk\psi_{k}:

𝐚|m⟩=m|m−1⟩,𝐚∗|m⟩=m+1|m+1⟩.\displaystyle{\bf a}\left\lvert m\right\rangle=\sqrt{m}\left\lvert m-1\right\rangle,\qquad{\bf a}^{*}\left\lvert m\right\rangle=\sqrt{m+1}\left\lvert m+1\right\rangle.

In particular the following identity holds: 𝐍=𝐚∗​𝐚{\bf N}={\bf a}^{*}{\bf a}.

It can be easily checked that both 𝐐{\bf Q} and 𝐏{\bf P} have Gaussian distribution with respect to the vacuum state |0⟩\left\lvert 0\right\rangle. In fact they are ‘jointly Gaussian’

⟨0|exp(iu𝐐+iv𝐏)||0⟩=exp(−14(u2+v2)).\left\langle 0\right|\exp(iu{\bf Q}+iv{\bf P})|\left|0\right\rangle=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4}(u^{2}+v^{2})\right).

We will often use the complex form of the unitary Weyl operators

W⁡(z):=exp⁡(z​𝐚∗−z¯​𝐚)=exp⁡(i​p0​𝐐−i​q0​𝐏),z=(q0+i​p0)/2∈ℂ,W(z):=\exp(z{\bf a}^{*}-\bar{z}{\bf a})=\exp(ip_{0}{\bf Q}-iq_{0}{\bf P}),\qquad z=(q_{0}+ip_{0})/\sqrt{2}\in\mathbb{C},

which satisfy the Weyl relations

W​(z)∗​W​(z′)​W​(z)=exp⁡(2​i​Im​(z¯′​z))​W​(z′).W(z)^{*}W(z^{\prime})W(z)=\exp\left(2i{\rm Im}(\bar{z}^{\prime}z)\right)W(z^{\prime}).

The coherent (vector) states |z⟩\left|z\right\rangle are obtained by displacing the vacuum state with Weyl operators

|z⟩:=W(z)|0⟩=exp(−|z|2/2)∑m=0∞zmm!|m⟩.\left|z\right\rangle:=W(z)\left|0\right\rangle=\exp(-|z|^{2}/2)\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{m}}{\sqrt{m!}}\left|m\right\rangle. (4.12)

They are Gaussian states with the same variance as the vacuum, and means ⟨z|𝐐|z⟩=2Re(z)\left\langle z\right|{\bf Q}\left|z\right\rangle=\sqrt{2}{\rm Re}(z) and ⟨z|𝐏|z⟩=2Im(z)\left\langle z\right|{\bf P}\left|z\right\rangle=\sqrt{2}{\rm Im}(z):

⟨z|W(z′)|z⟩=exp(−12|z−z′|2+2iIm(z¯′z)).\left\langle z\right|W(z^{\prime})\left|z\right\rangle=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}|z-z^{\prime}|^{2}+2i{\rm Im}(\bar{z}^{\prime}z)\right).

Besides, coherent states, an important role in our discussion will be played by the thermal equilibrium states. For every β>0\beta>0 we define the Gaussian state

ϕβ​(W⁡(z))=exp⁡(−|z|22​tanh⁡(β/2)).\phi_{\beta}(W(z))=\exp\left(-\frac{|z|^{2}}{2\tanh(\beta/2)}\right). (4.13)

Its density matrix consisting of a mixture of kk-photon states with geometrical weights

Φβ=(1−e−β)∑k=0∞e−k​β|k⟩⟨k|.\Phi_{\beta}=(1-e^{-\beta})\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-k\beta}\left|k\right\rangle\left\langle k\right|. (4.14)

and can also be obtained by ’smearing’ the coherent states with a Gaussian kernel:

Φβ=eβ−1π∫ℂexp(−(eβ−1)|z|2)|z⟩⟨z|dz.\Phi_{\beta}=\frac{e^{\beta}-1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\exp\left(-(e^{\beta}-1)|z|^{2}\right)\left|z\right\rangle\left\langle z\right|dz. (4.15)

The thermal equilibrium states can be shifted in ‘phase space’ by means of displacement operations DzD^{z} which act by adjoining with unitaries W⁡(z)W(z), i.e.

Dz​(⋅):=Ad⁡[W⁡(z)]​(⋅)=W​(z)∗⋅W⁡(z).D^{z}(\cdot):={\rm Ad}[W(z)](\cdot)=W(z)^{*}\cdot W(z).

The result is a Gaussian state ϕβz\phi^{z}_{\beta} with the same variance as ϕβ\phi_{\beta} and the same means as |z⟩|z\rangle:

ϕβz​(W⁡(z′)):=exp⁡(−|z|22​tanh⁡(β/2)+2​i​Im​(z¯′​z)),Φβz:=Dz​(Φβ):=W​(z)∗​Φβ​W​(z).\phi^{z}_{\beta}(W(z^{\prime})):=\exp\left(-\frac{|z|^{2}}{2\tanh(\beta/2)}+2i{\rm Im}(\bar{z}^{\prime}z)\right),\qquad\Phi_{\beta}^{z}:=D^{z}(\Phi_{\beta}):=W(z)^{*}\Phi_{\beta}W(z). (4.16)

4.3 The multimode Fock space and the limit Gaussian shift experiment

We now consider d⁡(d−1)/2d(d-1)/2 commuting harmonic oscillators, with a joint state consisting of independent Gaussian states. Let us define the multimode Fock space

ℱ:=⨂1≤j<k≤dL2​(ℝ),\mathcal{F}:=\bigotimes_{1\leq j<k\leq d}L^{2}(\mathbb{R}),

in which we identify the number basis

|𝐦⟩=⨂j<k|mj,k⟩,𝐦={mj,k∈ℕ:j<k}.\left|{\bf m}\right\rangle=\bigotimes_{j<k}\left|m_{j,k}\right\rangle,\qquad{\bf m}=\left\{m_{j,k}\in\mathbb{N}:j<k\right\}. (4.17)

For each of the oscillators we define the thermal equilibrium state

Φj,k:=Φβj,k,βj,k=ln⁡(μj/μk),\Phi_{j,k}:=\Phi_{\beta_{j,k}},\qquad\beta_{j,k}=\ln(\mu_{j}/\mu_{k}), (4.18)

where {μ1,…,μd}\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}\} are the eigenvalues of the density matrix ρ0\rho_{0} (cf. (4.1)). We now use the Weyl operators to displace these states by an amount proportional to the off-diagonal elements ζj,k\zeta_{j,k} of ρθ\rho^{\theta} (cf. (4.2) and (4.4))

Φj,kζj,k:=W​(ζj,k2​μj−μk)∗​Φj,k​W​(ζj,k2​μj−μk).\Phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}}:=W\left(\frac{\zeta_{j,k}}{2\sqrt{\mu_{j}-\mu_{k}}}\right)^{*}\,\Phi_{j,k}\,W\left(\frac{\zeta_{j,k}}{2\sqrt{\mu_{j}-\mu_{k}}}\right).

We now define the joint state ϕζ→\phi^{\vec{\zeta}} of the oscillators with density matrix

Φζ→=⨂j<kΦj,kζj,k∈𝒯1​(ℱ),\Phi^{\vec{\zeta}}=\bigotimes_{j<k}\Phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F}), (4.19)

where 𝒯1​(ℱ)\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F}) is the space of trace-class operators on ℱ\mathcal{F}.

The states Φζ→\Phi^{\vec{\zeta}} form the quantum part of the limit Gaussian experiment. The classical part is identical to the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Gaussian shift model N⁡(u→,V⁡(μ))N(\vec{u},V(\mu)) of Example 3.5, where μ={μ1,…,μd}\mu=\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}\}.

Definition 4.2.

On the algebra L∞​(ℝd−1)⊗ℬ⁡(ℱ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}) we define normal state ϕθ\phi^{\theta} with density

Φθ:=𝒩⁡(u→,V⁡(μ))⊗Φζ→∈L1​(ℝd−1)⊗𝒯1​(ℱ),\Phi^{\theta}:=\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V(\mu))\otimes\Phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F}), (4.20)

where 𝒩⁡(u→,V⁡(μ))\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V(\mu)) is the Gaussian density of Example 3.5. The quantum-classical Gaussian experiment ℛ\mathcal{R} is defined by

ℛ={Φθ:θ=(u→,ζ→)∈ℝd−1×ℂd⁡(d−1)/2}.\mathcal{R}=\{\Phi^{\theta}:\theta=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta})\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2}\}.

4.4 The main theorem

We are now ready to formulate the main result of the paper. In view of subsequent application to optimal state estimation, it is essential to consider (slowly) growing domains of the local parameters. For given β,γ>0\beta,\gamma>0 we define

Θn,β,γ={(ζ→,u→):∥ζ→∥∞≤nβ,‖u→‖∞≤nγ}.\Theta_{n,\beta,\gamma}=\left\{(\vec{\zeta},\vec{u}):\lVert\vec{\zeta}\rVert_{\infty}\leq n^{\beta},\left\lVert\vec{u}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq n^{\gamma}\right\}.

Recall that δ\delta is the separation between the eigenvalues of ρ0\rho_{0} given by equation (4.1). Though we use parametrisation (4.4) for density matrices ρθ\rho_{\theta}, recall that in the first order this is approximated by ρ~θ\tilde{\rho}_{\theta} defined in (4.2). In fact it can be shown that the same theorem holds for the latter parametrisation.

Theorem 4.3.

Let δ>0\delta>0, let β<1/9\beta<1/9 and γ<1/4\gamma<1/4. Let the quantum experiments

𝒬n={ρθ,n:θ∈Θn,β,γ},ℛn={Φθ:θ∈Θn,β,γ},\mathcal{Q}_{n}=\left\{\rho^{\theta,n}:\theta\in\Theta_{n,\beta,\gamma}\right\},\qquad\mathcal{R}_{n}=\left\{\Phi^{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{n,\beta,\gamma}\right\},

where ρθ,n=ρθ/n⊗n\rho^{\theta,n}=\rho_{\theta/\sqrt{n}}^{\otimes n} is the state on M⁡((ℂd)⊗n)M\left((\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}\right) given by equation (4.4), and Φθ\Phi^{\theta} is given by (4.20).

Then, there exist channels (completely positive, normalised maps)

Tn\displaystyle T_{n} :\displaystyle: M​(ℂd)⊗n→L1​(ℝd−1)⊗𝒯1​(ℱ)\displaystyle M(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}\to L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F}) (4.21)
Sn\displaystyle S_{n} :\displaystyle: L1​(ℝd−1)⊗𝒯1​(ℱ)→M​(ℂd)⊗n\displaystyle L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F})\to M(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} (4.22)

with 𝒯1​(ℱ)\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F}) is the space of trace-class operators on ℱ\mathcal{F}, such that

supθ∈Θn,β,γ‖Φθ−Tn​(ρθ,n)‖1=O⁡(n−ϵ/δ),\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\lVert\Phi^{\theta}-T_{n}(\rho^{\theta,n})\right\rVert_{1}=O(n^{-\epsilon}/\delta), (4.23)
supθ∈Θn,β,γ‖Sn​(Φθ)−ρθ,n‖1=O⁡(n−ϵ/δ),\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\lVert S_{n}(\Phi^{\theta})-\rho^{\theta,n}\right\rVert_{1}=O(n^{-\epsilon}/\delta), (4.24)

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 depends only on δ\delta, β\beta and γ\gamma. In particular we have

limn→∞Δ⁡(𝒬n,ℛn)=0,\lim_{n\to\infty}\Delta(\mathcal{Q}_{n},\mathcal{R}_{n})=0,

where Δ⁡(⋅,⋅)\Delta(\cdot,\cdot) is the Le Cam distance defined in (2.5).

In other words, we get polynomial speed of convergence of the approximation, which is enough to build two-step evaluation strategies in the finite experiments globally asymptotically equivalent to strategies in the limit experiment [17].

4.5 The relation between LAN and CLT

One way to think of local asymptotic normality is the following: we would like to understand the asymptotic behaviour of the collective (fluctuation) observables (4.27) with respect to a whole neighborhood of the state ρ\rho, how the limit distribution changes as we change the reference state ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n}.

The quantum Central Limit Theorem describes the asymptotic behaviour of the same observables with respect to a fixed state, and is one of the ingredients in the proof of a different version of LAN based on weak convergence [16]. However, in the case of strong convergence, which is the object of this paper, CLT does not play any role since we are interested in convergence in norm rather than in distribution, and uniformly over a range of parameters.

The purpose of the section is to derive a ‘coordinate free’ version of the limit Gaussian experiment using the Central Limit Theorem and the notion of symmetric logarithmic derivative. The reader interested in the proof of main theorem can skip the following pages and continue with section 5.

4.5.1 Quantum Central Limit Theorem

Let ρ\rho be a fixed faithful state on M⁡(ℂd)M(\mathbb{C}^{d}). To ρ\rho we associate an algebra of canonical commutation relations carrying a Gaussian state ϕ\phi. The Quantum Central Limit Theorem [37] says that ϕ\phi is the limit distribution of certain multi-particle observables with respect to of product states ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n}.

Let

(A,B)ρ:=Tr⁡(ρ​A∘B),where​A∘B:=A​B+B​A2,(A,B)_{\rho}:=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\,A\circ B),\qquad{\rm where~}A\circ B:=\frac{AB+BA}{2},

be a positive inner product on the real linear space of selfadjoint operators M​(ℂd)s​aM(\mathbb{C}^{d})_{sa}. We define the Hilbert space with inner product (⋅,⋅)ρ(\cdot,\cdot)_{\rho}.

L2​(ρ)={A∈M​(ℂd)s​a:Tr⁡(A​ρ)=0}.L^{2}(\rho)=\{A\in M(\mathbb{C}^{d})_{sa}:{\rm Tr}(A\rho)=0\}.

Let σ\sigma be the symplectic form on L2​(ρ)L^{2}(\rho)

σ⁡(A,B)=i2​Tr​(ρ⁡[A,B]).\sigma(A,B)=\frac{i}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\,[A,B]).

The C∗C^{*}-algebra of canonical commutation relations C​C​R​(L2​(ρ),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho),\sigma) is generated by the Weyl operators W⁡(A)W(A) satisfying the relations

W(A)∗=W(−A),W(A)W(B)=W(A+B)exp(−iσ(A,B)),A,B∈L2(ρ).W(A)^{*}=W(-A),\qquad W(A)W(B)=W(A+B)\exp(-i\sigma(A,B)),\quad A,B\in L^{2}(\rho).

On C​C​R​(L2​(ρ),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho),\sigma) we define the Gaussian (quasifree) state

ϕ⁡(W⁡(A)):=exp⁡(−12​‖A‖ρ2),‖A‖ρ2=(A,A)ρ.\phi(W(A)):=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|A\|_{\rho}^{2}\right),\qquad\|A\|_{\rho}^{2}=(A,A)_{\rho}. (4.25)

The state ϕ\phi is regular, i.e. there exists a representation (π,ℋ)(\pi,\mathcal{H}) of the algebra C​C​R​(L2​(ρ),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho),\sigma) such that the one parameter family t↦π⁡(W⁡(t​A))t\mapsto\pi(W(tA)) is weakly continuous and ϕ\phi is a normal state on the von Neumann algebra generated by π⁡(C​C​R​(L2​(ρ),σ))\pi(CCR(L^{2}(\rho),\sigma)). This means that there exist selfadjoint ’field operators’ B⁡(A)B(A) such that π⁡(W⁡(t​A))=exp⁡(i​t​B​(A))\pi(W(tA))=\exp(itB(A)), and there exists a density matrix Φπ∈𝒯1​(ℋ)\Phi_{\pi}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H}) such that

ϕ⁡(W⁡(A))=Tr⁡(exp⁡(i​B​(A))​Φπ),A∈L2​(ρ).\phi(W(A))=\mathrm{Tr}\left(\exp(iB(A))\Phi_{\pi}\right),\qquad A\in L^{2}(\rho).

The representation (π,ℋ)(\pi,\mathcal{H}) can be obtained through the GNS construction, or by ‘diagonalising’ the CCR algebra as we will see in a moment. From (4.25) we deduce that the distribution of B⁡(A)B(A) with respect to ϕ\phi is a centred normal distribution with variance ‖A‖ρ2\|A\|_{\rho}^{2}. From the Weyl relations it follows that the fields satisfy the following canonical commutation relations

[B⁡(A),B⁡(C)]=2​i​σ​(A,C)​𝟏,A,C∈L2​(ρ).[B(A),B(C)]=2i\sigma(A,C)\mathbf{1},\qquad A,C\in L^{2}(\rho).

Consider now the tensor product ⨂k=1nM⁡(ℂd)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{n}M(\mathbb{C}^{d}) which is generated by elements of the form

A(k)=𝟏⊗⋯⊗A⊗⋯⊗𝟏,A^{(k)}=\mathbf{1}\otimes\dots\otimes A\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{1}, (4.26)

with AA acting on the kk-th position of the tensor product. We are interested in the asymptotics as n→∞n\to\infty of the joint distribution under the state ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n}, of ‘fluctuation’ elements of the form

Fn​(A):=1n​∑k=1nA(k).F_{n}(A):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}A^{(k)}. (4.27)
Theorem 4.4.

[Quantum CLT] Let A1,…,As∈L2​(ρ)A_{1},\dots,A_{s}\in L^{2}(\rho). Then the following holds

limn→∞Tr⁡(ρ⊗n​(∏l=1sFn​(Al)))=ϕ⁡(∏l=1s(B⁡(Al))),\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}{\rm Tr}\left(\rho^{\otimes n}\left(\prod_{l=1}^{s}F_{n}(A_{l})\right)\right)=\phi\left(\prod_{l=1}^{s}\left(B(A_{l})\right)\right),
limn→∞Tr⁡(ρ⊗n​(∏l=1sexp⁡(i​Fn​(Al))))=ϕ⁡(∏l=1sW⁡(Al)).\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}{\rm Tr}\left(\rho^{\otimes n}\left(\prod_{l=1}^{s}\exp(iF_{n}(A_{l}))\right)\right)=\phi\left(\prod_{l=1}^{s}W(A_{l})\right).

Although the algebra C​C​R​(L2​(ρ),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho),\sigma) may look rather abstract, its structure can be easily understood by ‘diagonalising’ it. Let us assume that ρ\rho is a diagonal matrix ρ0=Diag⁡(μ1,…,μd)\rho_{0}={\rm Diag}(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}). The Hilbert space L2​(ρ0)L^{2}(\rho_{0}) decomposes as direct sum of orthogonal subspaces ℋρ0⊕ℋρ0⟂\mathcal{H}_{\rho_{0}}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{\rho_{0}}^{\perp} where

ℋρ0:=Lin{A:[A,ρ0]=0,Tr(Aρ0)=0},andℋρ0⟂=Lin{Tj,k,j≠k},\mathcal{H}_{\rho_{0}}:={\rm Lin}\{A:[A,\rho_{0}]=0,{\rm Tr}(A\rho_{0})=0\},\quad{\rm and}\quad\mathcal{H}_{\rho_{0}}^{\perp}={\rm Lin}\{T_{j,k},j\neq k\}, (4.28)

with Tj,kT_{j,k} the generators of the 𝔰​𝔲​(d)\mathfrak{su}(d) algebra defined in (7.2).

(di,dj)ρ0=Tr⁡(ρ0​di​dj)=δi,j​μi−μi​μj=[V⁡(μ)]i,j,(d_{i},d_{j})_{\rho_{0}}={\rm Tr}(\rho_{0}d_{i}d_{j})=\delta_{i,j}\mu_{i}-\mu_{i}\mu_{j}=[V(\mu)]_{i,j},

where VμV_{\mu} is the covariance matrix (3.3).

Moreover

tj,k:=Tj,k/2​(μj−μk),j≠k,t_{j,k}:=T_{j,k}/\sqrt{2(\mu_{j}-\mu_{k})},\qquad j\neq k, (4.29)

σ(tj,k,tk,j)=−1/2,j<k,andσ(tj,k,tl,m)=0for{j,k}≠{l,m}.\sigma(t_{j,k},t_{k,j})=-1/2,\quad j<k,\quad{\rm and}~~\sigma(t_{j,k},t_{l,m})=0\quad{\rm for~}\{j,k\}\neq\{l,m\}.

which means that {tj,k,tk,j}\{t_{j,k},t_{k,j}\} generate isomorphic algebras of quantum harmonic oscillator which we denote by C​C​R​(ℂ)CCR(\mathbb{C}). From

‖tj,k‖ρ02=Tr⁡(ρ0​tj,k2)=μj+μk2​(μj−μk)\|t_{j,k}\|_{\rho_{0}}^{2}={\rm Tr}(\rho_{0}t_{j,k}^{2})=\frac{\mu_{j}+\mu_{k}}{2(\mu_{j}-\mu_{k})}

and (4.13) we conclude that each of the oscillators is prepared independently in the thermal equilibrium state ϕj,k=ϕβj,k\phi_{j,k}=\phi_{\beta_{j,k}} with βj,k=ln⁡(μj/μk)\beta_{j,k}=\ln(\mu_{j}/\mu_{k}).

Based on the discussion of sections 4.2 and 4.3 we can choose ℋ:=L2​(ℝd−1)⊗ℱ\mathcal{H}:=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{F} and define the regular representation π\pi of C​C​R​(L2​(ρ0),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho_{0}),\sigma) on this space in a straightforward way and its von Neumann completion is L∞​(ℝd−1)⊗ℬ⁡(ℱ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}). The state ϕ\phi decomposes as

ϕ≅N⁡(0,Vμ)⊗⨂j<kϕj,k.\phi\cong N(0,V_{\mu})\otimes\bigotimes_{j<k}\phi_{j,k}. (4.30)

which is precisely the state ϕθ\phi^{\theta} for θ=(u→,ζ→)=(0→,0→)\theta=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta})=(\vec{0},\vec{0}), defined in (4.20).

4.5.2 The quantum Gaussian shift experiment through Fisher information

We complete the family of states ϕθ\phi^{\theta} of the experiment ℛ\mathcal{R} by shifting ϕ0\phi^{{0}} with the help of symmetric logarithmic derivatives. As in the classical case, this will be a family of Gaussian states with the same covariance, and mean proportional to the local parameter θ\theta. The covariance is related to the Fisher information matrix as described in Remark 3.4. Thus we will start by defining the quantum analogues of the score functions and the Fisher information matrix for the full quantum model ρθ\rho_{\theta}.

Let us define the symmetric logarithmic derivatives [27, 28] as the solutions in L2​(ρ0)L^{2}(\rho_{0}) of

ℒj,k(r​e)∘ρ0=∂ρθ∂Re​ζj,k|θ=0,ℒj,k(i​m)∘ρ0=∂ρθ∂Im​ζj,k|θ=0,ℓi∘ρ0=∂ρθ∂ui|θ=0,\mathcal{L}_{j,k}^{(re)}\circ\rho_{0}=\left.\frac{\partial\rho_{\theta}}{\partial\,{\rm Re}\zeta_{j,k}}\right|_{\theta=0},\quad\mathcal{L}_{j,k}^{(im)}\circ\rho_{0}=\left.\frac{\partial\rho_{\theta}}{\partial\,{\rm Im}\zeta_{j,k}}\right|_{\theta=0},\quad\ell_{i}\circ\rho_{0}=\left.\frac{\partial\rho_{\theta}}{\partial u_{i}}\right|_{\theta=0},

Then with Hj,k,Ei,iH_{j,k},E_{i,i} defined in (7.2)

ℒj,k(r​e)=Hk,j/(μj+μk),ℒj,k(i​m)=Hj,k/(μj+μk),ℓi=Ei,i/μi−Ed,d/μd,\mathcal{L}_{j,k}^{(re)}=H_{k,j}/(\mu_{j}+\mu_{k}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{j,k}^{(im)}=H_{j,k}/(\mu_{j}+\mu_{k}),\quad\ell_{i}=E_{i,i}/\mu_{i}-E_{d,d}/\mu_{d},

and the quantum Fisher information matrix consists of a ‘classical block’ that coincides with that of the classical multinomial model in (3.2)

[Iρ0]i​j:=(ℓi,ℓj)ρ0=[I⁡(μ)]i​j,1≤i,j≤d−1,[I_{\rho_{0}}]_{ij}:=(\ell_{i},\ell_{j})_{\rho_{0}}=[I(\mu)]_{ij},\qquad 1\leq i,j\leq d-1,

and a ‘purely quantum’ block given by the diagonal matrix

Hρ0=Diag(∥ℒj,k∥ρ02,∥ℒk,j∥ρ02:j<k)=Diag((μj+μk)−1,(μj+μk)−1:j<k).H_{\rho_{0}}={\rm Diag}\left(\|\mathcal{L}_{j,k}\|_{\rho_{0}}^{2},\|\mathcal{L}_{k,j}\|_{\rho_{0}}^{2}:j<k\right)={\rm Diag}\left((\mu_{j}+\mu_{k})^{-1},(\mu_{j}+\mu_{k})^{-1}:j<k\right).
Lemma 4.5.

Let

ℒ⁡(θ):=∑j<k(Re⁡(ζj,k)​ℒj,k(r​e)+Im⁡(ζj,k)​ℒj,k(i​m))+∑iui​ℓi,θ=(u→,ζ→).\mathcal{L}(\theta):=\sum_{j<k}\left({\rm Re}(\zeta_{j,k})\mathcal{L}^{(re)}_{j,k}+{\rm Im}(\zeta_{j,k})\mathcal{L}^{(im)}_{j,k}\right)+\sum_{i}u_{i}\ell_{i},\qquad\theta=(\vec{u},\vec{\zeta}).

Consider the representation (π,ℋ)(\pi,\mathcal{H}) of C​C​R​(L2​(ρ0),σ)CCR(L^{2}(\rho_{0}),\sigma) and the normal state ϕ\phi on L∞​(ℝd−1)⊗ℬ⁡(ℱ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}) as defined in the previous section (cf. 4.30). Let ϕ~θ\tilde{\phi}^{\theta} be the state defined by

ϕθ(W(A)):=exp(−12∥A,A∥ρ0+i(A,ℒ(θ))ρ0),A∈L2(ρ0).\phi^{\theta}(W(A)):=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|A,A\|_{\rho_{0}}+i(A,\mathcal{L}(\theta))_{\rho_{0}}\right),\qquad A\in L^{2}(\rho_{0}). (4.31)

Then ϕ~θ\tilde{\phi}^{\theta} is normal with respect to the representation (π,ℋ)(\pi,\mathcal{H}) and coincides with ϕθ\phi^{\theta} (cf. (4.20)).

A=∑j<k(uj,k​tj,k+vj,k​tk,j)+∑iwi​ℓi,A=\sum_{j<k}\left(u_{j,k}t_{j,k}+v_{j,k}t_{k,j}\right)+\sum_{i}w_{i}\ell_{i},

where we used the following expression for the displaces thermal equilibrium states ϕj,kζj,k=ϕβz\phi_{j,k}^{\zeta_{j,k}}=\phi_{\beta}^{z} defined in (4.16), with β=ln⁡μj/μk,z=ζj,k\beta=\ln\mu_{j}/\mu_{k},z=\zeta_{j,k}

5 Explicit form of the channels and first steps of the proof

5.1 Second look at the irreducible representations of S​U​(d)SU(d)

Before explaining the steps involved in the proof, let us take a closer look at the block states (4.9). Recall that we have the decomposition of Theorem 4.1 over Young diagrams with nn boxes and

ρθ,n=⨁λρλθ,n⊗𝟏𝒦λMn​(λ).\rho^{\theta,n}=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\otimes\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}}}{M_{n}(\lambda)}.

Let {f1,…,fd}\{f_{1},\dots,f_{d}\} be the eigenvectors of ρ0\rho_{0}, i.e. the standard basis vectors of ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}. Then the eigenvectors of ρ0⊗n=ρ0,n\rho_{0}^{\otimes n}=\rho^{0,n} are tensor products

f𝐚:=fa⁡(1)⊗fa⁡(2)⊗⋯⊗fa⁡(n),f_{\bf a}:=f_{a(1)}\otimes f_{a(2)}\otimes\dots\otimes f_{a(n)},

and the eigenvalues ∏kλa⁡(k)\prod_{k}\lambda_{a(k)} do not depend on the order of the vectors in the product.

5.1.1 Projecting onto a copy of ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}.

Our aim is to ‘project’ to an irreducible representation ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} and obtain an explicit expression for the eigenvectors of the block components ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}. Such a projection is not unique, in fact for any rank one operator |v⟩​⟨u|∈ℬ⁡(𝒦λ)|v\rangle\langle u|\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}) with ⟨u|v⟩=1\langle u|v\rangle=1 we can define a (not necessarily orthogonal) projection y=y2y=y^{2} on a copy of ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}

yλ​(u,v):=𝟏ℋλ⊗|v⟩​⟨u|:(ℂd)⊗n→ℋλ⊗|v⟩.\displaystyle y_{\lambda}(u,v):=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}}\otimes|v\rangle\langle u|:(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}\to\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes|v\rangle.

However the action of yλ​(u,v)y_{\lambda}(u,v) on basis vectors f𝐚f_{\bf a} depends on a particular identification between (ℂd)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} and the direct sum in Theorem 4.1. Therefore we need a direct way of defining such a projection and the key observation is that yλ​(u,v)y_{\lambda}(u,v) is a minimal projection in the algebra Alg(π~d(τ):τ∈S(n)){\rm Alg}(\tilde{\pi}_{d}(\tau):\tau\in S(n)), i.e. it cannot be decomposed into a sum of non-zero projections, and vice-versa any minimal projection is of this form. The following recipe (given without proof) shows how to construct minimal projections in the S⁡(n)S(n) group algebra. We recall that the group ∗-algebra 𝒜⁡(S⁡(n))\mathcal{A}(S(n)) is the linear space spanned by the group elements endowed with a product stemming from the group product

a=∑τ∈S⁡(n)a⁡(τ)​τ,b=∑ϱ∈S⁡(n)b⁡(ϱ)​ϱ⟹a​b=∑τ,ϱ∈S⁡(n)a⁡(τ)​b​(ϱ)​τ​ϱ=∑σ∈S⁡(n)(∑s∈S⁡(n)a⁡(σ​s−1)​b​(s))​σ,a=\sum_{\tau\in S(n)}a(\tau)\tau,\quad b=\sum_{\varrho\in S(n)}b(\varrho)\varrho~\Longrightarrow~ab=\sum_{\tau,\varrho\in S(n)}a(\tau)b(\varrho)\tau\varrho=\sum_{\sigma\in S(n)}\left(\sum_{s\in S(n)}a(\sigma s^{-1})b(s)\right)\sigma,

and with adjoint a∗=∑τ∈S⁡(n)a⁡(τ)​τ−1a^{*}=\sum_{\tau\in S(n)}a(\tau)\tau^{-1}.

Let λ\lambda be a Young diagram with nn boxes consider the (standard) Young tableau tt in which the boxes are filled with the numbers {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} in increasing order from left to right along rows, starting with the top row and ending with the bottom row, as shown in the left-side tableau of Figure 2.

Define the group algebra elements

Pλ=∑σ∈ℛλσ,Qλ=∑τ∈𝒞λsgn⁡(τ)​τ,P_{\lambda}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{R}_{\lambda}}\sigma,\qquad Q_{\lambda}=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}{\rm sgn}(\tau)\tau,

where ℛλ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda} is the S⁡(n)S(n)-subgroup of permutation leaving the rows of tt invariant, and 𝒞λ\mathcal{C}_{\lambda} is the subgroup of permutations leaving the columns of tt invariant. Note that PλP_{\lambda} and QλQ_{\lambda} are self-adjoint elements of the S⁡(n)S(n) group algebra satisfying

5.1.2 Finding a basis in ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}

By the previous Theorem the vectors yλ​f𝐚y_{\lambda}f_{\bf a} span ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}, but are not linearly independent. A semistandard Young tableau is a diagram filled with numbers in {1,…,d}\{1,\dots,d\} such that the entries are non-decreasing along rows from left to right and increasing along columns from top to bottom, as in the right-side of Figure 2.

Theorem 5.2.
