5.2 Description of TnT_{n}

We look for channels

Tn:M⁡((ℂd)⊗n)→L1​(ℝd−1)⊗𝒯1​(ℱ)T_{n}:M((\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n})\to L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1})\otimes\mathcal{T}_{1}(\mathcal{F})

of the form:

Tn:ρθ,n⟼∑λpλθ,n​τλn⊗(Vλ​ρλθ,n​Vλ∗).T_{n}:\rho^{\theta,n}\longmapsto\sum_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\,\tau_{\lambda}^{n}\otimes\left(V_{\lambda}\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}^{*}\right). (5.12)

Here, VλV_{\lambda} is an isometry from ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} to ℱ\mathcal{F}, i.e. Vλ∗​Vλ=𝟏ℋλV_{\lambda}^{*}V_{\lambda}=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}}. On the classical side, τλn\tau_{\lambda}^{n} is a probability law on ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1}. We may view τn\tau^{n} as a Markov kernel (2.2) from the set of diagrams λ\lambda to ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1}.

The channel TnT_{n} can be described by the following sequence of operations. We first performs a ‘which block’ measurement over the irreducible representations and get a result λ\lambda. Then, on the one hand, we apply a classical randomization to λ\lambda, and on the other hand we apply a channel depending on our result λ\lambda to the conditional state ρλ\rho_{\lambda}.

The underlying ideas are the following.

1). The probability distribution pλθ,np_{\lambda}^{\theta,n} is essentially a multinomial depending only on u→\vec{u}, as it can be deduced from (5.9) and (5.7). As we have seen in Example 3.5, this converges (in Le Cam sense) to a classical Gaussian shift experiment. Here, in order to obtain the strong norm convergence we need to smooth the discrete distribution into a continuous one with respect to the Lebesgue measure. We choose a particular smoothing distribution which will insure the uniform L1L^{1} convergence to the Gaussian model (Lemma 6.1).

Definition 5.3.

Let τλn\tau^{n}_{\lambda} be the probability density on ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1} defined for all λ\lambda such that ∑λi=n\sum\lambda_{i}=n, by:

τλn​(d​x)=τλn​(x)​d​x=d​x​n(d−1)/2​χ​(Aλ,n),\displaystyle\tau^{n}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{d}x)=\tau^{n}_{\lambda}(x)\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{d}x\,n^{(d-1)/2}\chi(A_{\lambda,n}), (5.13)

where Aλ,n={x∈ℝd−1:|n1/2xi+nμi−λi|≤1/2,1≤i≤d−1}A_{\lambda,n}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}:\ |n^{1/2}x_{i}+n\mu_{i}-\lambda_{i}|\leq 1/2,1\leq i\leq d-1\}. We further denote

bλθ,n=pλθ,n​τλn,b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}=p_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\tau^{n}_{\lambda},

depending on θ\theta only through u→\vec{u}.

2). For the quantum part, we map the ‘finite-dimensional vacuum’ |𝟎,λ⟩|{\bf 0},\lambda\rangle to the Fock space vacuum |𝟎⟩\left\lvert{\bf 0}\right\rangle, and the basis vectors |𝐦,λ⟩|{\bf m},\lambda\rangle of ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} ‘near’ the basis vectors |𝐦⟩|{\bf m}\rangle of the Fock space ℱ\mathcal{F} (cf. definitions (5.2) and respectively (4.17)). Here we need to tackle the problem that {|𝐦,λ⟩}\{|{\bf m},\lambda\rangle\} is not an orthonormal basis but only becomes so asymptotically. The following lemma provides the isometry VλV_{\lambda} appearing in (5.12).

Lemma 5.4.

Let η<2/9\eta<2/9. Suppose that λi−λi+1≥δ​n\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i+1}\geq\delta n for all 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, with the convention λd+1=0\lambda_{d+1}=0. Then for n>n0​(η,δ,d)n>n_{0}(\eta,\delta,d) there exists an isometry Vλ:ℋλ→ℱV_{\lambda}:\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\to\mathcal{F} such that, V|𝟎,λ⟩=|𝟎⟩V|{\bf 0},\lambda\rangle=|{\bf 0}\rangle and for |𝐦|≤nη|\mathbf{m}|\leq n^{\eta},

⟨𝐦|Vλ=11+(C~​n)(9​η−2)/12/δ1/3⟨𝐦,λ|\left\langle\mathbf{m}\right|V_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\tilde{C}n)^{(9\eta-2)/12}/\delta^{1/3}}}\left\langle\mathbf{m},\lambda\right|

where C~=C~​(η,d)\tilde{C}=\tilde{C}(\eta,d) is a particular constant. More precisely, n0n_{0} can be taken of the form (C⁡(d)/δ2)1/(1−3​η)(C(d)/\delta^{2})^{1/(1-3\eta)}.

Proof. See section 7.2. The main tool is Lemma 7.3.

∎

For Young diagrams which do not satisfy the assumption of the previous Lemma, the isometry VλV_{\lambda} can be defined arbitrarily. The reason is that fact that those blocks have vanishing collective weight and can be neglected altogether (cf. Lemma 6.2).

From this operational description we conclude that TnT_{n} is a proper channel since τn\tau^{n} is a Markov kernel and VλV_{\lambda} is an isometry. We then want to prove that Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n)T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}) is close to Φ𝟎\Phi^{\bf 0} and that the finite-dimensional operations Δλζ→,n\Delta_{\lambda}^{\vec{\zeta},n} have almost the same action as the displacement operators DζD^{\zeta} of the Fock space, cf. (4.16). Finite-dimensional coherent states and formula 4.15 will be the stepping stone to those results.

6 Main steps of the proof

6.1 Why TnT_{n} does the work

We shall break (4.23) in small manageable pieces. The result and brief explanatory remarks, repeating those in the derivation, are given from (6.3) on.

We introduce first a few shorthand notations: the restriction of TnT_{n} to the block λ\lambda is

Tλ:ρλθ,n↦Vλ​ρλθ,n​Vλ∗,T_{\lambda}:\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\mapsto V_{\lambda}\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}^{*},

so that

Tn:ρθ,n↦∑λpλθ,n​τλn⊗Tλ​(ρλθ,n)=∑λbλθ,n⊗ϕλθ,n.\displaystyle T_{n}:\rho^{\theta,n}\mapsto\sum_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\tau^{n}_{\lambda}\otimes T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda})=\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\phi^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}.

We also define Tλ∗:ϕ↦Vλ∗​ϕ​VλT_{\lambda}^{*}:\phi\mapsto V_{\lambda}^{*}\phi V_{\lambda}. and note that Tλ∗​Tλ=IdℋλT_{\lambda}^{*}T_{\lambda}={\rm Id}_{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}}.

We expand (5.12) as

Tn​(ρθ,n)\displaystyle T_{n}(\rho^{\theta,n}) =∑λbλθ,n⊗ϕλθ,n\displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}
=N⁡(u→,Vμ)⊗ϕζ→−(N⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)⊗ϕζ→−∑λbλθ,n⊗(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n).\displaystyle=N(\vec{u},V_{\mu})\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\left(N(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right).

Proving (4.23) then amounts to proving

supθ∈Ωn,ϵ‖(N(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)⊗ϕζ→+∑λbλθ,n⊗(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1≤Cn−ϵ/δ.\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\epsilon}}\left\|\left(N(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}+\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}\leq Cn^{-\epsilon/\delta}.

We now use the triangle inequality to upper bound this norm by a sum of “elementary” terms to be treated separately in the following sections.

‖(𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)⊗ϕζ→+∑λbλθ,n⊗(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1≤\displaystyle\left\|\left(\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}+\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}\leq
‖(𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)⊗ϕζ→‖1+∑λ‖bλθ,n⊗(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1≤\displaystyle\left\|\left(\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\right\|_{1}+\sum_{\lambda}\left\|b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\otimes\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}\leq
‖ϕζ→‖1​‖(𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)‖1+∑λ‖bλθ,n‖1​‖(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1.\displaystyle\left\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\right\|_{1}\left\|\left(\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}+\sum_{\lambda}\left\|b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right\|_{1}\left\|\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}.

Since ‖ϕζ→‖1=‖𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)‖1=‖ϕλθ,n‖=1\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\|_{1}=\|\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})\|_{1}=\|\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\|=1, we have ‖(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1≤2\left\|\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1}\leq 2. Similarly ∑λ‖bλθ,n‖1=1\sum_{\lambda}\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1}=1 because ‖bλθ,n‖1=pλθ,n\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1}=p_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}. We split the sum over λ\lambda in two parts, one for which it is expected that ‖(ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n)‖1\left\|\left(\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1} is small, and the other on which the sum of all ‖bλθ,n‖1\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1} is small. Specifically, define the set of typical Young diagrams

Λn,α:={λ:|λi−nμi|≤nα,1≤i≤d},forα>1/2,\Lambda_{n,\alpha}:=\{\lambda:|\lambda_{i}-n\mu_{i}|\leq n^{\alpha},1\leq i\leq d\},\qquad{\rm for}~\alpha>1/2, (6.1)

then

‖Tn​(ρθ,n)−𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)⊗ϕζ→‖≤\displaystyle\left\|T_{n}(\rho^{\theta,n})-\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})\otimes\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\right\|\leq
‖𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n‖1+supλ∈Λn,α‖ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n‖1+2​∑λ∉Λn,α‖bλθ,n‖1.\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right\|_{1}+\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right\|_{1}+2\sum_{\lambda\not\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1}. (6.2)

The first term corresponds to the convergence of the classical experiment in the Le Cam sense. If the second term is small, then on Λn,α\Lambda_{n,\alpha}, the (purely quantum) family ρλθ,n\rho^{\theta,n}_{\lambda} is near the family ϕζ→\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}. The last term corresponds to the other representations. If it is small, it means that there is concentration of pλθ,np_{\lambda}^{\theta,n} around the representations with shape λi=n​μi\lambda_{i}=n\mu_{i}. In other words, the only representations that matter are those in Λn,α\Lambda_{n,\alpha}, there is almost no mass on the other representations.

The hardest term to dominate (notice that the two others are classical) is the second. We transform it until we reach tractable fragments.

‖ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n‖1\displaystyle\left\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right\|_{1} =‖ϕζ→−Tλ​(ρλθ,n)‖1\displaystyle=\left\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}(\rho_{\lambda}^{\theta,n})\right\|_{1}
=‖Dζ→​(ϕ0→)−[Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗]​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n))‖1\displaystyle=\left\|D^{\vec{\zeta}}(\phi^{\vec{0}})-[T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}))\right\|_{1}
=‖Dζ→​(ϕ0→)−Dζ→​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n))+Dζ→​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n))−[Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗]​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n))‖1\displaystyle=\left\|D^{\vec{\zeta}}(\phi^{\vec{0}})-D^{\vec{\zeta}}(T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}))+D^{\vec{\zeta}}(T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}))-[T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}))\right\|_{1}
≤‖Dζ→​(ϕ0→)−Dζ→​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n))‖1+‖[Dζ→−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗]​(Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n)−ϕ0→)‖1+‖[Dζ→−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗]​(ϕ0→)‖1\displaystyle\begin{split}&\leq\left\|D^{\vec{\zeta}}(\phi^{\vec{0}})-D^{\vec{\zeta}}(T_{\lambda}(\rho^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda}))\right\|_{1}+\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](T_{\lambda}(\rho^{{\vec{0}},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda})-\phi^{\vec{0}})\right\|_{1}\\ &\quad+\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\phi^{\vec{0}})\right\|_{1}\end{split}
≤3​‖Tλ​(ρλ0→,u→,n)−ϕ0→‖1+‖[Dζ→−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗]​(ϕ0→)‖1\displaystyle\leq 3\left\|T_{\lambda}(\rho^{{\vec{0}},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda})-\phi^{\vec{0}}\right\|_{1}+\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\phi^{\vec{0}})\right\|_{1}

where in the last inequality we used the fact that the displacement operators are isometries.

Note that the first term does not depend on ζ→\vec{\zeta} and the second term is small if the displacement operators Δλζ→,n\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda} and Dζ→D^{\vec{\zeta}} have ‘similar action’ on an appropriate domain. Using the integral formula (4.15) for gaussian states ϕβ\phi_{\beta} and the fact that ϕ0→\phi^{\vec{0}}, is a tensor product of such states (cf. (4.34)) we bound the second term by

‖[Dζ→−TλΔλζ→,nTλ∗](ϕ0→)‖1≤∫ℂd⁡(d−1)/2f(z→)‖[Dζ→−TλΔλζ→,nTλ∗](|z→⟩⟨z→|)‖1dz→\displaystyle\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\phi^{\vec{0}})\right\|_{1}\leq\int_{\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2}}f(\vec{z})\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|\vec{z}\right\rangle\left\langle\vec{z}\right|)\right\|_{1}d\vec{z}

where

f⁡(z→)=∏i<jμi−μjπ​μj​exp⁡(−μi−μjμj​|zi,j|2).f(\vec{z})=\prod_{i<j}\frac{\mu_{i}-\mu_{j}}{\pi\mu_{j}}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{i}-\mu_{j}}{\mu_{j}}|z_{i,j}|^{2}\right).

and |z→⟩⟨z→|=Dz→(|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)\left|\vec{z}\right\rangle\left\langle\vec{z}\right|=D^{\vec{z}}(\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|) is the multimode coherent state, so

Now, ff is a probability density, and the norm in the integrand is dominated by two. By splitting the integral we obtain

By adding and subtracting additional terms

Dζ→​Dz→−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗​Dz→=\displaystyle D^{\vec{\zeta}}D^{\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}D^{\vec{z}}= Dζ→+z→−Tλ​Δλζ→+z→,n​Tλ∗\displaystyle D^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}
+Tλ​Δλζ→+z→,n​Tλ∗−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Δλz→,n​Tλ∗\displaystyle+T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}
+Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Δλz→,n​Tλ∗−Tλ​Δλζ→,n​Tλ∗​Dz→.\displaystyle+T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}D^{\vec{z}}.

we deduce that

‖[Dζ→−TλΔλζ→,nTλ∗](|z→⟩⟨z→|)‖1\displaystyle\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|\vec{z}\right\rangle\left\langle\vec{z}\right|)\right\|_{1} ≤‖[Dζ→+z→−TλΔλζ→+z→,nTλ∗](|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1\displaystyle\leq\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|)\right\|_{1}
+‖[Δλζ→+z→,n−Δλζ→,nΔλz→,n](|𝟎,λ⟩⟨𝟎,λ|)‖1\displaystyle\quad+\left\|[\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}-\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}](|\bf{0},\lambda\rangle\langle\bf{0},\lambda|)\right\|_{1}
+‖[Δλz→,nTλ∗−Tλ∗Dz→](|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1\displaystyle\quad+\left\|[\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}-T_{\lambda}^{*}D^{\vec{z}}](\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|)\right\|_{1}

where the last two terms on the right side have been simplified using properties of Tλ,Tλ∗,Δλζ→,nT_{\lambda},T^{*}_{\lambda},\Delta_{\lambda}^{\vec{\zeta},n}. Notice that the first and third norms are essentially the same and the three terms are small if the action of Δλζ→\Delta_{\lambda}^{\vec{\zeta}} is mapped into that of the displacement operators Dζ→D^{\vec{\zeta}}.

Putting all this together, our ‘expanded’ form for (4.23) is

supθ∈Ωn,β,γ‖Tn​(ρθ,n)−ϕζ→⊗𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)‖\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\|T_{n}(\rho^{\theta,n})-\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}\otimes\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})\right\| (6.3)
≤supθ∈Ωn,β,γ‖(𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n)‖1\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\|\left(\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right)\right\|_{1} (6.4)
+2supθ∈Ωn,β,γ∑λ∉Λn,α∥bθ,nλ∥1\displaystyle+2\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sum_{\lambda\not\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1} (6.5)
+3supθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖ϕ0→−Tλ(ρλ0→,u→,n)‖1\displaystyle+3\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|\phi^{{\vec{0}}}-T_{\lambda}(\rho^{{\vec{0}},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda})\right\|_{1} (6.6)
+sup‖z→‖≤nβsupθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖[Dζ→+z→−TλΔλζ→+z→,nTλ∗](|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1\displaystyle+\sup_{\|\vec{z}\|\leq n^{\beta}}\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|\mathbf{0}\right\rangle\left\langle\mathbf{0}\right|)\right\|_{1} (6.7)
+sup‖z→‖≤nβsupθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖[Dz→−TλΔλz→,nTλ∗](|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1\displaystyle+\sup_{\|\vec{z}\|\leq n^{\beta}}\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|[D^{\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{{\vec{z}},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|\mathbf{0}\right\rangle\left\langle\mathbf{0}\right|)\right\|_{1} (6.8)
+sup‖z→‖≤nβsupθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖[Δλζ→+z→,n−Δλζ→,nΔλz→,n](|𝟎,λ⟩⟨𝟎,λ|)‖1\displaystyle+\sup_{\|\vec{z}\|\leq n^{\beta}}\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|[\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}-\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}](\left|\mathbf{0},\lambda\right\rangle\left\langle\mathbf{0},\lambda\right|)\right\|_{1} (6.9)
+2∫‖z→‖≥nβf(z→)dz→.\displaystyle+2\int_{\|\vec{z}\|\geq n^{\beta}}f(\vec{z})\mathrm{d}\vec{z}. (6.10)

The last Gaussian tail term is less than C​exp⁡(−δ​n2​β)C\exp(-\delta n^{2\beta}) where CC depends only on the dimension dd. Under the hypothesis n2​β>2/δn^{2\beta}>2/\delta, this can be bounded again by O⁡(n−2​β)O(n^{-2\beta}).

The following lemmas provide upper bounds for each of the terms. Before each lemma we remind the reader what is the significance of the bound. The proofs are gathered in section 7.

The classical part of the channel is a Markov kernel τ\tau (see definition 5.3) mapping the ‘which block’ distribution pλθ,np_{\lambda}^{\theta,n} into the density bλθ,nb_{\lambda}^{\theta,n} on ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1} which is approaches uniformly the gaussian shift experiment (6.4). Recall that bλθ,nb_{\lambda}^{\theta,n} depends only on u→\vec{u} and not on ζ→\vec{\zeta}, so that we have the same parameter set for the two classical experiments.

Lemma 6.1.

With the above definitions, for any ϵ\epsilon, we have

supθ∈Ωn,β,γ‖𝒩(u→,Vμ)−∑λbλθ,n‖1=O(n−1/2+ϵ/δ,n−1/4+γ/δ).\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\|\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu})-\sum_{\lambda}b_{\lambda}^{\theta,n}\right\|_{1}=O\left(n^{-1/2+\epsilon}/\delta,n^{-1/4+\gamma}/\delta\right).

The next lemma deals with (6.5) by showing concentration around Young diagrams λ\lambda in the ‘typical subset’ (6.1). This allows we to restrict to this set of diagrams in further estimates.

Lemma 6.2.

Let α−γ−1/2>0\alpha-\gamma-1/2>0. Then, with the above definitions we have

supθ∈Ωn,β,γ∑λ∉Λn,α∥bλθ,n∥1=O(nd2exp(−n2​α−1/2)),\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sum_{\lambda\not\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\|b^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|_{1}=O\left(n^{d^{2}}\exp(-n^{2\alpha-1}/2)\right),

with the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) term converging to zero.

The term (6.6) shows that when the rotation parameter is zero, the block states ρλ0→,u→,n\rho_{\lambda}^{\vec{0},\vec{u},n} are essentially thermal equilibrium states, as one would expect from the quantum Central Limit Theorem 4.4. However the convergence here is in norm rather than in distribution, and uniform over the various parameters.

Lemma 6.3.

With the above definitions, we have

supθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖ϕ0→−Tλ(ρλ0→,u→,n)‖1=O(n−1/2+γ+η/δ,n(9​η−2)/24/δ1/6).\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|\phi^{{\vec{0}}}-T_{\lambda}(\rho^{{\vec{0}},\vec{u},n}_{\lambda})\right\|_{1}=O(n^{-1/2+\gamma+\eta}/\delta,\,n^{(9\eta-2)/24}/\delta^{1/6}).

The terms (6.7) and (6.8) show that the ‘finite dimensional coherent states’ obtained by performing small rotations on the ‘finite-dimensional vacuum’ are uniformly close to their infinite dimensional counterparts, thus justifying the coherent state terminology.

Lemma 6.4.

Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be such that 2​β+ϵ≤η<2/92\beta+\epsilon\leq\eta<2/9.

Then,

sup‖z→‖≤nβsup∥ξ→∥≤n−1/2+2β/δsupθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖[Dζ→+z→−TλΔλζ→+z→,ξ→,nTλ∗](|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1=R(n)\sup_{\|\vec{z}\|\leq n^{\beta}}\,\sup_{\|\vec{\xi}\|\leq n^{-1/2+2\beta}/\delta}\,\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\,\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\,\left\|[D^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z}}-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},\vec{\xi},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}](\left|\mathbf{0}\right\rangle\left\langle\mathbf{0}\right|)\right\|_{1}=R(n)

with

R(n)2=O(n(9​η−2)/12δ−1/3,n−1+2​β+ηδ−1,n−1/2+3β+2ϵδ−3/2,n−1+α+2​βδ−1,OPENn−1+α+η​δ−1,n−1+3​η​δ−1,n−β)R(n)^{2}=O\left(n^{(9\eta-2)/12}\delta^{-1/3},n^{-1+2\beta+\eta}\delta^{-1},n^{-1/2+3\beta+2\epsilon}\delta^{-3/2},n^{-1+\alpha+2\beta}\delta^{-1},\right.\\ \left.n^{-1+\alpha+\eta}\delta^{-1},n^{-1+3\eta}\delta^{-1},n^{-\beta}\right) (6.11)

For estimating the terms (6.7, 6.8), the case when ξ→=0→\vec{\xi}=\vec{0} is sufficient. This more general form is useful for the proof of Lemma 6.5. The unitary operation is defined as Δλζ→,ξ,n:=Ad⁡[Uλ​(ζ→,ξ,n)]\Delta_{\lambda}^{\vec{\zeta},\xi,n}:={\rm Ad}[U_{\lambda}(\vec{\zeta},\xi,n)] with 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁U⁡(ζ→,ξ,n))U(\vec{\zeta},\xi,n)) the general S​U​(d)SU(d) element of (7.1).

Finally (6.9) shows that the ‘finite-dimensional’ displacement operators multiply as the corresponding displacement operators when acting on the vacuum.

Lemma 6.5.

With the above definitions, under the same hypotheses as in Lemma 6.4, we have

sup‖z→‖≤nβsupθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α‖[Δλζ→+z→,n−Δλζ→,nΔλz→,n](|𝟎,λ⟩⟨𝟎,λ|)‖1=R(n)\sup_{\|\vec{z}\|\leq n^{\beta}}\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\left\|[\Delta^{\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}-\Delta^{\vec{\zeta},n}_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{z},n}_{\lambda}](|\bf{0},{\lambda}\rangle\langle\bf{0},{\lambda}|)\right\|_{1}=R(n)

with R⁡(n)R(n) given by equation (6.11).

From the last three lemmas, together with the bound on the remainder integral (6.10) we obtain the following lemma which can be plugged into the bound (6.2):

Lemma 6.6.

With the above notations under the same hypotheses as in Lemma 6.4, we have

supθ∈Ωn,β,γsupλ∈Λn,α∥ϕζ→−ϕλθ,n∥=R(n)+O(n−1/2+γ+η/δ+n(9​η−2)/24/δ1/6)\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{n,\alpha}}\|\phi^{\vec{\zeta}}-\phi^{\theta,n}_{\lambda}\|=R(n)+O(n^{-1/2+\gamma+\eta}/\delta+n^{(9\eta-2)/24}/\delta^{1/6})

with R⁡(n)R(n) given by equation (6.11).

Gathering all these results yield the following theorem which provides the bound (4.23).

Theorem 6.7.

For any δ>0\delta>0, 1>α>1/21>\alpha>1/2, η<2/9\eta<2/9, ϵ>0\epsilon>0, β<(η+ϵ)/2\beta<(\eta+\epsilon)/2, γ<1/4\gamma<1/4, the sequence of channels TnT_{n} satisfies

supθ∈Ωn,β,γ‖Tn(ρθ,n)−ϕ‖1=O(n−1/2+β+η/2δ−1/2+n−1/4+β/2δ−1/4+n−1/2+α/2+η/2δ−1/2+n−1/2+3η/2δ−1/2+n−β/2+n−1/2+γ+η/δ+n(9​η−2)/24/δ1/6)\sup_{\theta\in\Omega_{n,\beta,\gamma}}\left\|T_{n}(\rho^{\theta,n})-\phi\right\|_{1}=O(n^{-1/2+\beta+\eta/2}\delta^{-1/2}+n^{-1/4+\beta/2}\delta^{-1/4}+n^{-1/2+\alpha/2+\eta/2}\delta^{-1/2}+\\ n^{-1/2+3\eta/2}\delta^{-1/2}+n^{-\beta/2}+n^{-1/2+\gamma+\eta}/\delta+n^{(9\eta-2)/24}/\delta^{1/6}) (6.12)

With any explicit α,β,γ,δ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta, we get an explicit polynomial rate.

6.2 Definition of SnS_{n} and proof of its efficiency

The channel SnS_{n} is essentially the inverse of TnT_{n} and as we shall see, (4.24) can be deduced from (4.23).

On the classical side we need a Markov kernel completing the equivalence between the family pλu→,np_{\lambda}^{\vec{u},n} and 𝒩⁡(u→,Vμ)\mathcal{N}(\vec{u},V_{\mu}). Let σn\sigma^{n} be defined by

σn:x∈ℝd−1↦δλx\sigma^{n}:x\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\mapsto\delta_{\lambda_{x}} (6.13)

where λx\lambda_{x} is the Young diagram such that ∑1dλi=n\sum_{1}^{d}\lambda_{i}=n, and |n1/2​xi+n​μi−λi|<1/2|n^{1/2}x_{i}+n\mu_{i}-\lambda_{i}|<1/2, for 2≤i≤d2\leq i\leq d. No such diagram exists, we set λx\lambda_{x} to any admissible value, for example (n,0,…,0)(n,0,\dots,0). Notice that with (5.13), σn∘τn∘σn=σn\sigma^{n}\circ\tau^{n}\circ\sigma^{n}=\sigma^{n}. 7 Technical proofs

7.1 Combinatorial and representation theoretical tools

Here we continue the analysis of the S​U​(d)SU(d) irreducible representations (πλ,ℋλ)(\pi_{\lambda},\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}) started in section 5.1. The purpose of this section is to provide good estimates of quantities of the type ⟨𝐦,λ​∣πλ​(U)∣​𝐥,λ⟩\langle\mathbf{m},{\lambda}\mid\pi_{\lambda}(U)\mid\mathbf{l},{\lambda}\rangle which will be needed in the proofs of Lemmas 7.3 and 6.4.

We shall use the following form of a general S​U​(d)SU(d) element and the shorthand notations

U⁡(ζ→,ξ→)\displaystyle U(\vec{\zeta},\vec{\xi}) :⁣=\displaystyle:= exp⁡[i⁡(∑i=1d−1ξi​Hi+∑1≤j<k≤dRe⁡(ζj,k)​Tj,k+Im⁡(ζj,k)​Tk,jμj−μk)],\displaystyle\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\xi_{i}H_{i}+\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq d}\frac{{\rm Re}(\zeta_{j,k})T_{j,k}+{\rm Im}(\zeta_{j,k})T_{k,j}}{\sqrt{\mu_{j}-\mu_{k}}}\right)\right],
U⁡(ζ→,ξ→,n)\displaystyle U(\vec{\zeta},\vec{\xi},n) :⁣=\displaystyle:= U⁡(ζ→/n,ξ→/n),U⁡(ζ→):=U⁡(ζ→,0→),U⁡(ζ→,n):=U⁡(ζ→/n),\displaystyle U(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n},\vec{\xi}/\sqrt{n}),\quad U(\vec{\zeta}):=U(\vec{\zeta},\vec{0}),\quad U(\vec{\zeta},n):=U(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n}), (7.1)

where HiH_{i} and Ti,jT_{i,j} are the generators of S​U​(d)SU(d) defined by

Hj\displaystyle H_{j} =\displaystyle= Ej,j−Ej+1,j+1for​j≤d−1;\displaystyle E_{j,j}-E_{j+1,j+1}\qquad\text{for}~j\leq d-1;
Tj,k\displaystyle T_{j,k} =\displaystyle= i​Ej,k−i​Ek,jfor​1≤j<k≤d;\displaystyle iE_{j,k}-iE_{k,j}\qquad\text{for}~1\leq j<k\leq d;

Γ⁡(f𝐚):=|𝐦|−#⁡{1≤c≤λ1:t𝐚c≠Idc},\Gamma({f_{\bf a}}):=|{\bf m}|-\#\{1\leq c\leq\lambda_{1}:{t_{\bf a}^{c}}\neq{\rm Id}^{c}\},

𝒪λ​(𝐦)​⋂𝒱=⋃Γ∈ℕ𝒱Γ​(𝐦).\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}({\bf m})\bigcap\mathcal{V}=\bigcup_{\Gamma\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}^{\Gamma}({\bf m}).

Note that Γ⁡(f𝐚)≥0\Gamma(f_{\bf a})\geq 0 and is zero if and only if each column t𝐚c{t_{\bf a}^{c}} is either Idc{\rm Id}^{c} or of the form t𝐚c​(r)=j​δr=i+r​δr≠i{t_{\bf a}^{c}}(r)=j\delta_{r=i}+r\delta_{r\neq i} for some i≤l⁡(c)<ji\leq l(c)<j. A t𝐚c{t_{\bf a}^{c}} of this form will be called an (i,j)(i,j)-substitution.

The following ‘algorithm’ shows how to build all the possible f𝐚∈𝒱Γ​(𝐦){f_{\bf a}}\in\mathcal{V}^{\Gamma}({\bf m}), thus enabling us to estimate the size of 𝒱Γ​(𝐦)\mathcal{V}^{\Gamma}({\bf m}).

Algorithm

Let (𝐦,λ)({\bf m},\lambda) be fixed but otherwise arbitrary. In order to generate a particular admissible f𝐚∈𝒪λ​(𝐦)f_{\bf a}\in\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}({\bf m}) we need to select the mi,jm_{i,j} boxes on row ii which are filled with jj, for all i<ji<j. The rest of the boxes are filled automatically with ii’s. The constraint is that no column should have two boxes filled with the same number.

Generating a diagram can be described intuitively as follows. We start with the ‘vacuum’ vector (tableau) f𝟎:=f𝐦=𝟎f_{\bf 0}:=f_{{\bf m}={\bf 0}} (row ii is filled exclusively with ii’s), and with a set of |𝐦||{\bf m}| bricks containing mi,jm_{i,j} identical bricks labelled (i,j)(i,j), for each pair i<ji<j. To change the content of a box from ii into jj we place an (i,j)(i,j)-brick in that box. This procedure is repeated until all bricks have been used, each box being modified at most once.

At this stage each column cc may contain several bricks placed in the appropriate boxes, so that its configuration is uniquely defined by the set of bricks κ{\kappa} which shall be called a column-modifier. For example if κ={(i,j),(f,l)}{\kappa}=\{(i,j),(f,l)\} then the column has entries

t𝐚c​(k)={jif k=i;lif k=f;kotherwise.t_{\bf a}^{c}(k)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}j&\textrm{if $k=i$};\\ l&\textrm{if $k=f$};\\ k&\textrm{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.

Note that a column-modifier is not an arbitrary collection of bricks but one that can be used to produce a column with different entries. In the previous example, if i<fi<f this means either (j≠fj\neq f and j,l>l⁡(c)j,l>l(c)) or (j=fj=f and l>l⁡(c)l>l(c)). The elementary one-brick column-modifier denoted κ⁡(i,j){\kappa}(i,j) can only be used in a column with i≤l⁡(c)<ji\leq l(c)<j, otherwise the entry jj would appear twice.

Now, since the length of a column is at most dd and all entries must be different, there are less than d!d! different types of column-modifiers. Another important remark is that a column-modifier always increases the value of the modified cells, so that in this case t𝐚c​({1,…,l⁡(c)})≠{1,…,l⁡(c)}{t_{\bf a}^{c}}(\{1,\dots,l(c)\})\neq\{1,\dots,l(c)\}.

Alternatively to the above scenario where the bricks are inserted sequentially, we can first cluster them into |𝐦|−Γ|{\bf m}|-\Gamma column-modifiers, and then apply each column-modifier to a particular column. A given collection of column-modifiers is uniquely determined by {mκ:κ}\{m_{{\kappa}}:{\kappa}\} where mκm_{{\kappa}} is the multiplicity of κ{\kappa}. This procedure is detailed in the following 3 stages:

  1. I.

    Choose Γ\Gamma bricks among our |𝐦||{\bf m}|. As we have d⁡(d−1)/2d(d-1)/2 different types of bricks (recall that i>ji>j), and we do not distinguish between identical bricks, there are at most [d⁡(d−1)/2]Γ[d(d-1)/2]^{\Gamma} possibilities. For Γ=0\Gamma=0, we have only one choice.

  2. II.

    Consider the remaining bricks as a set of elementary column-modifiers. Starting from these, we sequentially add each of the Γ\Gamma bricks selected in the first stage, to one of these elementary column-modifiers to form non-elementary ones. At each step we have at most d!d! different types of column modifiers to which we can attach the new brick. Note that we do not distinguish between column modifiers of the same type, but rather consider them as an unordered set. Hence, we have less that (d!)Γ(d!)^{\Gamma} possibilities.

    Note that at the end of stage II at least max⁡{0,|𝐦|−2​Γ}\max\{0,|{\bf m}|-2\Gamma\} of the column-modifiers are elementary, and that mκ⁡(i,j)≤mi,jm_{{\kappa}(i,j)}\leq m_{i,j}.

  3. III.

    Apply the column-modifiers to the columns of f𝟎{f_{\bf 0}}, so that no two modifiers are applied to the same column and the resulting f𝐚∈𝒪λ​(𝐦){f_{\bf a}}\in\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}({\bf m}) is admissible. By construction Γ⁡(f𝐚)=Γ\Gamma(f_{\bf a})=\Gamma and all admissible tableaux can be generated in this way.

For counting the number of possibilities for the third stage we apply the column modifiers sequentially, but since some of them may be identical we need to divide by the combinatorial factor ∏κmκ!\prod_{{\kappa}}m_{{\kappa}}!, where mκm_{{\kappa}} is the number of column modifiers of type κ{\kappa}.

We distinguish between elementary column modifiers of type κ⁡(i,j){\kappa}(i,j) and composite ones. There are less than n possibilities of inserting a composite column-modifier κ{\kappa}. An elementary one of type κ⁡(i,j){\kappa}(i,j) can only be inserted in a column with at least ii rows, and since the resulting vector has to be admissible, the column cannot contain another jj, so its length is smaller than jj. There are λi−λj\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j} such columns. Hence the number of possibilities at stage three of the algorithm is upper bounded by

∏κ≠κ⁡(i,j)nmκmκ!⋅∏i<j(λi−λj)mκ⁡(i,j)mκ⁡(i,j)!.\displaystyle\prod_{{\kappa}\neq{\kappa}({i,j})}\frac{n^{m_{{\kappa}}}}{m_{{\kappa}}!}\cdot\prod_{i<j}\frac{(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{m_{{\kappa}(i,j)}}}{m_{{\kappa}(i,j)}!}. (7.4)

When Γ=0\Gamma=0, for each elementary column modifier κ⁡(i,j){\kappa}(i,j) the number of available columns is at least (λi−λj−|𝐦|)+:=max{0,λi−λj−|𝐦|}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}-\lvert{\bf m}|)_{+}:=\max\{0,\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}-\lvert{\bf m}|\}. Thus we have the following lower bound

∏i<j(λi−λj−|𝐦|)+mi,jmi,j!.\displaystyle\prod_{i<j}\frac{(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}-|\mathbf{m}|)_{+}^{m_{i,j}}}{m_{i,j}!}. (7.5)

Notice that the upper bound (7.4) depends on the set of multiplicities {mκ}\{m_{{\kappa}}\}.

We now return to our list of notations and definitions.

7) To each column of t𝐚t_{\bf a} we associated a column modifier which completely determines its content. If mκ𝐚m_{{\kappa}}^{\bf a} is the number of columns with column-modifer κ{\kappa}, we collect all multiplicities in E:={mκ𝐚:κ}.E:=\{m_{{\kappa}}^{\bf a}:{\kappa}\}. In particular Γ\Gamma is a function of EE

Γ⁡(f𝐚)=|𝐦|−∑κmκ𝐚.\Gamma(f_{\bf a})=|{\bf m}|-\sum_{{\kappa}}m_{{\kappa}}^{\bf a}.

Vectors for which Γ⁡(f𝐚)=0\Gamma(f_{\bf a})=0 have the same multiplicity set E0E^{0} where mκ⁡(i,j)=mi,jm_{{\kappa}(i,j)}=m_{i,j} for all i<ji<j and the other mκ=0m_{\kappa}=0. Similarly to 𝒱Γ​(𝐦)\mathcal{V}^{\Gamma}({\bf m}), we denote by 𝒱E​(𝐦)\mathcal{V}^{E}({\bf m}) the set of tableaux in 𝒪λ​(𝐦)​⋂𝒱\mathcal{O}_{\lambda}({\bf m})\bigcap\mathcal{V} with E⁡(f𝐚)=EE(f_{\bf a})=E, in particular

𝒱Γ​(𝐦)=⋃E𝒱E​(𝐦)\mathcal{V}^{\Gamma}({\bf m})=\bigcup_{E}\mathcal{V}^{E}({\bf m})

8) To each column cc of t𝐚t_{\bf a} we associate two disjoint sets: the added entries {t𝐚c​(1),…,t𝐚c​(l⁡(c))}∖{1,…,l⁡(c)}\{t_{\bf a}^{c}(1),\dots,t_{\bf a}^{c}(l(c))\}\setminus\{1,\dots,l(c)\} and the deleted entries {1,…,l⁡(c)}∖{t𝐚c​(1),…,t𝐚c​(l⁡(c))}\{1,\dots,l(c)\}\setminus\{t_{\bf a}^{c}(1),\dots,t_{\bf a}^{c}(l(c))\}. This data is placed into a single set by attaching a ±\pm sign to each entry, indicating if it is added or deleted. It is easy to verify that if t𝐚t_{\bf a} is admissible, the set of added and deleted entries is uniquely determined by the column-modifer κ{\kappa} associated to cc, and hence shall be denoted by S⁡(κ)S({\kappa}). For example S⁡(κ⁡(i,j))={(i,−),(j,+)}S({\kappa}(i,j))=\{(i,-),(j,+)\} and for κ={(i,j),(j,k)}{\kappa}=\{(i,j),(j,k)\} we have S⁡(κ)={(i,−),(k,+)}S({\kappa})=\{(i,-),(k,+)\}. We define the multiplicities mS𝐚=∑κ:S⁡(κ)=Smκ𝐚m_{S}^{\bf a}=\sum_{{\kappa}:S({\kappa})=S}m_{{\kappa}}^{\bf a} and F⁡(f𝐚):={mS𝐚:S}F(f_{\bf a}):=\{m_{S}^{\bf a}:S\} . =∏1≤c≤λ1∑sc∈Scϵ⁡(sc)​∏1≤r≤l⁡(c)Ut𝐚c​(r),t𝐛c​(sc​(r))\displaystyle=\prod_{1\leq c\leq\lambda_{1}}\sum_{{s_{c}}\in S_{c}}\epsilon({s_{c}})\prod_{1\leq r\leq{l(c)}}U_{{t_{\bf a}^{c}}(r),{t_{\bf b}^{c}}({s_{c}}(r))}
=∏1≤c≤λ1det(Ut𝐚c,t𝐛c).\displaystyle=\prod_{1\leq c\leq\lambda_{1}}\det(U^{{t_{\bf a}^{c}},{t_{\bf b}^{c}}}).

Proof of (7.8). The number of admissible f𝐚{f_{\bf a}} such that Γ⁡(f𝐚)=0\Gamma({f_{\bf a}})=0 is given by the products of the possibilities at each stage of the algorithm. For the first two stages, there is exactly one possibility when Γ=0\Gamma=0. Hence #​𝒱0\#\mathcal{V}^{0} is the number of possibilities at the third stage. Here the upper bound (7.4) reads as ∏j>i(λi−λj)mi,j/mi,j!\prod_{j>i}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{m_{i,j}}/m_{i,j}!. On the other hand, we may use (7.5) as a lower bound, recalling that λi−λj≥δ​n/2\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}\geq\delta n/2 and |𝐦|≤nη|{\bf m}|\leq n^{\eta} (cf. (7.7)). This yields the result (7.8).

Proof of (7.9). The number of f𝐚{f_{\bf a}} in 𝒱E\mathcal{V}^{E} is given by the third stage of the algorithm (the two first stages yield a particular EE). We then obtain (7.9) by applying (7.4) and neglecting the mκ!m_{{\kappa}}! factors, while noticing that ∑κmκ=|𝐦|−Γ\sum_{{\kappa}}m_{{\kappa}}=|\mathbf{m}|-\Gamma.

#​𝒱E≤n−Γ​δ−2​Γ​|𝐦|2​Γ​∏j>i(λi−λj)mi,jmi,j!,∀E​with​Γ​(E)=Γ.\#\mathcal{V}^{E}\leq n^{-\Gamma}\delta^{-2\Gamma}|\mathbf{m}|^{2\Gamma}\prod_{j>i}\frac{(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{m_{i,j}}}{m_{i,j}!},\qquad\forall E~{\rm with}~\Gamma(E)=\Gamma.

Proof of (5). We applying (7.6) with U=𝟏U=\mathbf{1}. Here we denote by t𝐚c​([1,l⁡(c)]){t_{\bf a}^{c}}([1,l(c)]) the set of entries {t𝐚c​(1),…,t𝐚c​(l⁡(c))}\{{t_{\bf a}^{c}}(1),\dots,{t_{\bf a}^{c}}(l(c))\}.

Now, since a modified column cannot satisfy t𝐚c​([1,l⁡(c)])=[1,l⁡(c)]{t_{\bf a}^{c}}([1,l(c)])=[1,l(c)] (and the same for 𝐛{\bf b}), the vectors f𝐚{f_{\bf a}} and f𝐛{f_{\bf b}} are orthogonal unless they have the same number of modified columns. Recall that the state ρθ,n:=ρθ/n⊗n\rho^{\theta,n}:=\rho^{\otimes n}_{\theta/\sqrt{n}} has the decomposition over ‘blocks’ λ\lambda given by (4.8). The probability distribution over Young diagrams pλζ→,u→,np_{\lambda}^{\vec{\zeta},\vec{u},n} depends only on the diagonal parameters u→\vec{u} and is given by

cnλ=(nλ1,λ2,…,λd)​∏l=1dλl!​∏k=l+1d(λl−λk+k−l)(λl+d−l)!.c_{n}^{\lambda}={n\choose\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{d}}\prod_{l=1}^{d}\frac{\lambda_{l}!\prod_{k=l+1}^{d}(\lambda_{l}-\lambda_{k}+k-l)}{(\lambda_{l}+d-l)!}.

The above formula can be understood as follows. Each eigenprojector carries a weight ∏i=1d(μu→,n)mi\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\mu^{\vec{u},n})^{m_{i}} where mim_{i} is the multiplicity of the vector fif_{i} in the tensor product f𝐚f_{\bf a}. Thus, we only need to add all multiplicities over vectors that are ‘inside’ the block λ\lambda. Since the irreducible representation has basis f𝐦f_{\bf m} labelled by semistandard Young tableaux, we get a factor

∏i=1d(μiu→,n)mi=∏i=1d(μiu→,n)λi​∏j=i+1d(μju→,nμiu→,n)mi,j.\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\mu_{i}^{\vec{u},n})^{m_{i}}=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\mu_{i}^{\vec{u},n})^{\lambda_{i}}\prod_{j=i+1}^{d}\left(\frac{\mu_{j}^{\vec{u},n}}{\mu_{i}^{\vec{u},n}}\right)^{m_{i,j}}.

The additional factor cnλc_{n}^{\lambda} is the dimension of 𝒦λ\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}, on which the state is proportional to the identity.

Recall that μiu→,n=μi+ui/n\mu_{i}^{\vec{u},n}=\mu_{i}+u_{i}/\sqrt{n} for 1≤i≤(d−1)1\leq i\leq(d-1) and μdu→,n=μd−(∑iui)/n\mu_{d}^{\vec{u},n}=\mu_{d}-(\sum_{i}u_{i})/\sqrt{n}. Moreover mi,j≤nm_{i,j}\leq n for all (i,j)(i,j), so the total number of 𝐦{\bf m}’s is smaller than nd2n^{d^{2}}. Thus

∑𝐦∏i<j(μu→,n)λi​(μju→,nμiu→,n)mi,j≤nd2.\sum_{{\bf m}}\prod_{i<j}(\mu^{\vec{u},n})^{\lambda_{i}}\,\left(\frac{\mu_{j}^{\vec{u},n}}{\mu_{i}^{\vec{u},n}}\right)^{m_{i,j}}\leq n^{d^{2}}.

The key is to notice that, as we are dealing with a group, there is a rr such that

≤\displaystyle\leq ‖|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|−|r→⟩⟨r→|‖1+‖|r→⟩⟨r→|−TλΔλr→,s→,nTλ∗(|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|)‖1+∥Tλ(|𝟎,λ⟩⟨𝟎,λ|)−|𝟎⟩⟨𝟎|∥1.\displaystyle\left\|\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|-\left|\vec{r}\right\rangle\left\langle\vec{r}\right|\right\|_{1}+\left\|\left|\vec{r}\right\rangle\left\langle\vec{r}\right|-T_{\lambda}\Delta^{\vec{r},\vec{s},n}_{\lambda}T_{\lambda}^{*}(\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|)\right\|_{1}+\|T_{\lambda}(\left|{\bf 0},\lambda\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0},\lambda\right|)-\left|{\bf 0}\right\rangle\left\langle{\bf 0}\right|\|_{1}.

By continuity of the product, if x→,y→∈ℂd⁡(d−1)/2\vec{x},\vec{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{d(d-1)/2} are small enough, then U⁡(−x→−y→)​U​(x→)​U​(y→)∈𝒞U(-\vec{x}-\vec{y})U(\vec{x})U(\vec{y})\in\mathcal{C}. Since ‖ζ→‖+‖z→‖/n≤nβ−1/2/δ\|\vec{\zeta}\|+\|\vec{z}\|/\sqrt{n}\leq n^{\beta-1/2}/\delta, we can apply this to x→=ζ→/n,y→=z→/n\vec{x}=\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n},\vec{y}=\vec{z}/\sqrt{n} for n>(C/δ)11/2−βn>(C/\delta)^{\frac{1}{1/2-\beta}} with the constant CC depending only on the dimension, and get

(r→/n,s→/n)=f(ζ→/n,z→/n):=log[U(−(ζ→+z→)/n)U(ζ→/n)U(z→/n)].(\vec{r}/\sqrt{n},\vec{s}/\sqrt{n})=f(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n},\vec{z}/\sqrt{n}):=\log\left[U(-(\vec{\zeta}+\vec{z})/\sqrt{n})U(\vec{\zeta}/\sqrt{n})U(\vec{z}/\sqrt{n})\right].

Since ff is a C∞C^{\infty} function we can expand in Taylor series and it is easy to show that f⁡(0,0)=0f(0,0)=0, the first order partial derivatives are zero as well, and the second order derivatives are uniformly bounded in a neighbourhood of the origin. Thus we get

r→=nO(‖zi,j‖2n⁡(μi−μj),‖ζi,j‖2n⁡(μi−μj))=O(n−1/2+2β/δ).\vec{r}=\sqrt{n}\,O\left(\frac{\|z_{i,j}\|^{2}}{n(\mu_{i}-\mu_{j})},\frac{\|\zeta_{i,j}\|^{2}}{n(\mu_{i}-\mu_{j})}\right)=O(n^{-1/2+2\beta}/\delta).

∎
